By ANNABEL FENWICK ELLIOTT, COLUMNIST
Updated: 06:03 EST, 19 November 2026
Something very big and very bad is going to happen soon, I can just feel it. And the whispers I’m hearing from friends in high places imply I’m not wrong.
I used to scoff at ‘preppers’. I’ve always considered myself immune to doomsday scaremongering - and I thought all those billionaires who’ve been busy building survival bunkers in recent decades were just silly.
Furthermore, I do not subscribe to climate hysteria and I was fervently anti-lockdown during Covid. Even when the majority of the world was panic-buying loo roll and bolting themselves inside, I was unfazed. It seemed to me a gross overreaction and I haven’t changed my position on that. That pandemic was merely a dress rehearsal, I sense, for something much worse.
Today, I am beyond suspicious that something major is brewing.
Am I really to believe that a global Microsoft outage, the grounding of every plane in America, millions of US bank customers locked out of their accounts and Apple Pay going down – all in the space of six days – are mere coincidences? Officially, they were all tech ‘glitches’. Forgive me if I’m not reassured. Add to that the fact that hackers have been switching off supermarket freezers across Europe – are these not ominous precursors?
My husband, who usually shares the same laissez-faire attitude as I do, is feeling nervous too. He’s been in charge of our stockpiling.
So far we have six tanks for drinking water, several bricks of matches and fire-starters, a set of walkie talkies (I’m still not sure I see the point in those), a bow and arrow (yes, really) and enough non-perishable food to sustain us for many months.
Annabel Fenwick Elliott and her husband have begun stockpiling items for a doomsday scenario
Today, I am beyond suspicious that something major is brewing, she writes
I can’t believe it is only by chance that nations across the planet have all been issuing ‘advice’ on how to prepare for some sort of catastrophe in recent months.
At least 33 countries have so far announced guidelines encouraging households to stockpile food, drinking water and essential supplies – from central Europe and the Nordics to the US, Japan and South Korea.
Britain launched its ‘Be Ready’ campaign last month, advising every household to stash three days of essentials – a battery radio and a first aid kit among them – and Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has told the public to be ‘alert but not alarmed’.
Considering we had virtually no government warning before Covid closed the world down for several years, and politicians were darting around like headless chickens trying to make sense of it all, I find it very odd that now, all of a sudden, the powers-that-be are actively raising the red flags. As if they actually know something this time.
Why is Jacob Rees-Mogg on my Instagram feed talking about a hypothetical disaster, suggesting – as the UK Government has – that I withdraw cash, or (and I had to chuckle at this) ‘if you’re really desperate, some gold sovereigns’?
I spoke to one friend who runs a bank and shares my worries that ‘something big will happen’. He pointed out that it’s economically perilous for large numbers of people to suddenly dash to the ATM. If enough people do it, financial institutions go bust and a whopper of a recession soon follows. Governments know this – indeed, they’ve been guiding us into ever more cash-free behaviour for years – so they must have a very good reason to be telling us recently to ‘keep a little cash at home’.
Lo and behold, this week saw customers at some of America’s biggest banks locked out of online services as outages hit Chase, Wells Fargo, Bank of America and several other financial institutions. There was a similar disruption to Barclays in the UK.
Suddenly those nutters who keep their entire fortunes hidden in notes stuffed inside mattresses no longer seem so paranoid. I use Monzo, an exclusively online bank. I can only withdraw a few hundred pounds per day from cash points and I’ve started doing so regularly to build up a reserve.
While I don’t think, as some experts suggest, that ‘extreme weather’ is going to tip us into an immediate disaster, I do worry about AI.
Indeed, I asked a senior software engineer about the likelihood of a major tech-related incident, bad enough for us to stockpile, and he said that there was nothing to suggest imminent disaster, but it is inevitable that AI will trigger ever more regular cyber attacks.
Elon Musk, who is arguably one of the most intelligent and well-informed people in the world, puts the odds of it ending humanity at one in five. And he does seem to be in rather a rush to set up a new civilisation on Mars.
I’ll be honest, I used to fantasise about an apocalypse and the end of the mundane, tax-laden hamster wheel of our modern existence. It’s my favourite genre of fiction. Years of watching The Walking Dead, World War Z and Contagion have armed me with tips and convinced me I’d fare quite well.
Before having children Annabel used to 'fantasise' about an apocalypse, but says that the 'imminent' reality of a Doomsday situation now feels horrifying
And while ethically I was against the Covid lockdowns, it was from a selfish standpoint the best phase of my life. I hunkered down in the middle of the countryside with my dog and now-husband, worked from home in my pyjamas and when we were permitted to travel, enjoyed crowd-free minibreaks. I’m an introvert: socialising was illegal. It was glorious.
That was before I had children. The prospect of societal collapse no longer looks so thrilling. In fact, it appears hugely inconvenient at best and horrifyingly dangerous at worst. And for the first time in my life, it feels imminent.
Some years ago, I interviewed astrobiology research scientist Dr Lewis Dartnell, who authored The Knowledge: How to Rebuild our World After an Apocalypse. Eerily, he predicted ‘a particularly virulent strain of flu’ shortly before Covid broke out and warned me that ‘individually, we are astoundingly ignorant of even the basics of the production of food, shelter, clothes, medicine, materials or vital substances'.
He told me we would ‘very soon turn violent in competition for resources’ and remarked: ‘The theory goes, we’re only really three days away from rioting.’ Three days, incidentally, is the length of time the UK Government has told us to stockpile for. More wary preppers are gearing up for a lot longer than that.
As for me? Perhaps I need therapy, not more lentils, because I keep finding myself drifting further into nihilism – thinking things like ‘there’s no point in booking a holiday next year, the world will be over’. As for my husband, he’s spent all morning researching the best manufacturer of solar batteries (it’s Anker, apparently) and the most robust fermentation jars (Kilner).
I know we’re not alone in this horrible sense of dread. Nor do we feel ready for what’s to come. So – and I never thought I’d ask this – if any of you have tips on how to further ‘prep’ for widespread disaster, do leave them in the comments box below. I’m one of you now.

articles.title_orig: California attorney general subpoenas Nvidia over concerns about China and investor disclosures
articles.title_zh: California attorney general subpoenas Nvidia over concerns about China and investor disclosures
articles.content_orig:
California Attorney General Rob Bonta issued an investigative subpoena to Nvidia on Thursday as part of a probe of whether the company's advanced semiconductor chips ended up in China i n contravention of U.S. export restrictions, his office said.
The probe comes a week after former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned after allegations he had multiple affairs, including one with Alice Huang , a suspected Chinese spy. Alice Huang, who is not related to Jensen Huang, was an executive at Megaspeed , a Singapore-based company that is being investigation for potentially diverting restricted Nvidia chips to China.
"The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors," Bonta said in a statement.
"My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang's actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information — and if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law," Bonta said.
"Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors," the attorney general said.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Bonta's subpoena.
Nvidia shares are down 22% in the nine trading days since Huang admitted to an extramarital affair. The stock is on pace for its seventh straight weekly loss, shedding 38% of its value over that stretch.

The director of the Israeli spy agency Mossad is in Washington Friday for talks with senior Trump administration officials about the war in Iran , according to three sources with knowledge of the matter.
Why it matters : The visit by Roman Gofman, one of Benjamin Netanyahu's closest confidants, comes as the Israeli prime minister is pressing President Trump to resume the war against Iran.
Driving the news: Gofman is meeting with CIA Director John Ratcliffe, the sources said. He is also expected to travel to Miami to meet White House envoy Steve Witkoff, one of the sources said.
State of play: Trump has so far rejected pressure from Netanyahu to return to combat. The two discussed the Iran war during a Nov. 5 call, per a U.S. official.
The intrigue: Netanyahu has lost his majority in parliament after the Oct. 27 election in Israel.

articles.title_orig: Putin says Russia won't negotiate limited ceasefire with Ukraine after bridge strike
articles.title_zh: Putin says Russia won't negotiate limited ceasefire with Ukraine after bridge strike
articles.content_orig:
President Vladimir Putin said Thursday that Russia will not negotiate with Ukraine on a limited ceasefire, citing a Ukrainian strike this week on a major bridge connecting Russia and Ukraine's Russian-occupied Crimean Peninsula.
Putin made the remarks to reporters in Russian after meeting with President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China. He said he had discussed the possibility of a ceasefire in certain areas of Ukraine, but would not move forward with negotiations after Ukraine's strike on the Kerch Bridge, according to the Russian state news agencies.
The 12-mile bridge, which Putin ceremonially opened himself in 2018, is hugely symbolic as it links the Russian mainland with Crimea — territory that Russian forces occupied about four years earlier. The missile strike this week wasn't the first time Ukraine had targeted the piece of infrastructure, but it inflicted severe damage. Russia also struck two major bridges in Kyiv the same day.
Putin played down the bridge's strategic importance on Thursday and said he had heard the calls "from all sides" for a naval ceasefire or a suspension of strikes on energy facilities, but he ruled out direct negotiations with Ukraine, citing the attack on the bridge.
"Honestly, I discussed the issue with my colleagues at the Security Council, and I asked them to think about it and go back to the issue, so that we could reach some agreements," Putin said, according to Russian state news agency TASS. "However, we will not make agreements after strikes on the Crimean Bridge. We will respond to these strikes."
Putin vowed that Russia's retaliation for the strike on the bridge would be severe, TASS reported.
While Putin claims frequently to want peace, he denies that Russia started the war with his order for a full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, and Russia's attacks on Ukraine have been relentless.
It's not clear how much Ukraine came up in Mr. Trump's one-on-one meeting with Putin on Wednesday, or in the meeting with both Putin and Xi on Thursday. Last week, the White House said Ukraine wouldn't be a topic of discussion, but before he left for Asia, Mr. Trump said the three leaders would be discussing the war. The White House readout of the Trump-Xi-Putin meeting was sparse on detail, and did not mention Ukraine.
Meanwhile, Mr. Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner and U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff have been in Germany to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and the leaders of Germany, France, the U.K. and other European nations — a group known as the Coalition of the Willing — about Ukraine and other topics.
Kushner said they discussed the "latest efforts to achieve a just, lasting and durable peace in Ukraine."
"We are grateful for his leadership, constructive engagement, and close partnership as we work together toward our shared goal of ending this terrible war and building a secure and prosperous future for Ukraine and Europe," Kushner posted to X .
Merz, speaking to reporters after the meeting, called the China summit a photo-op and said the trilateral format "will not bring peace" in Ukraine.
As he went to shake Putin's hand before an earlier meeting Wednesday on the sidelines of the APEC summit in China, Mr. Trump referred to the Russian leader as "my friend."
"Who is he?" the president said, pointing at Putin and smiling. "He's my friend."

articles.title_zh: Trump Says He and China's Xi Want Moderate AI Rules

By DAVID WILCOCK, DEPUTY POLITICAL EDITOR and JASON GROVES, POLITICAL EDITOR
Published: 06:09 EST, 19 November 2026 | Updated: 08:59 EST, 19 November 2026
Andy Burnham will join European leaders in a show of solidarity with Ukraine today, hours after Donald Trump took part in an astonishing summit with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping .
The Prime Minister is chairing a meeting of 'Coalition of the Willing' countries in Berlin after announcing Britain will supply a further 1,000 long-range strike drones to Kyiv and jointly fund two £100 million attack boats with Norway.
But the meeting will have to deal with the fallout from the meeting between the leaders of the US, Russia and China in Shenzhen.
Ministers were already nervous that the US President could agree a stitch-up that weakens Ukraine as the war with Russia enters another winter.
He greeted Putin by describing him as a 'friend' with whom he was 'really making history', adding: 'No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.'
Putin, fresh from a setback in his war against Ukraine after the crippling of a key bridge linking Crimea to Russia, said the three countries have 'numerous shared interests in the settlement of regional conflicts, including obviously the conflict in Ukraine'.
The Prime Minister, pictured with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, will co-chair a meeting of 'Coalition of the Willing' countries in Berlin
But the meeting will have to deal with the fallout from the meeting between the leaders of the US, Russia and China in Shenzhen
Speaking in the Commons yesterday, Mr Burnham declined to comment on the Shenzhen summit directly, but said: 'When that meeting is taking place in China I will be in Berlin for a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing.
'The thing that we need to do is continue to stand squarely by Ukraine, and that is what this Government will do.'
He said that Britain was united in its support for Ukraine, adding: 'On this issue, let that clear message go out as that meeting takes place in China: this country is squarely with Ukraine.
'We know who the aggressor is in this situation, and we will not in any way deflect from continuing that support.'
The PM last night unveiled a £260million package of direct support for Ukraine.
The package includes 1,000 long-range drones capable of delivering heavy warheads to strike military targets at distances of more than 600 miles.
Putin, fresh from a setback in his war against Ukraine after the crippling of a key bridge linking Crimea to Russia, said the three countries have 'numerous shared interests'
The UK will also build and deliver maritime, logistical and surveillance drones to assist Ukraine in resupplying frontline forces with vital supplies like blood and fridges to hold medicines.
It follows agreement in recent days for Britain to bolster Ukraine's air defences and impose tighter sanctions on Russian oil producers.
The move comes as Putin targets civilian infrastructure in a bid to break Ukrainian morale during the cruel winter months when temperatures regularly drop to minus 20 degrees.
In recent weeks, Ukraine has faced more than 2,000 Russian attacks on its energy infrastructure, leaving civilians without heat or power.
In parts of the country, including the capital Kyiv, energy and water blackouts are now a daily occurrence, sometimes lasting up to 22 hours at a time as engineers battle to restore supplies.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said: 'Putin uses winter as a weapon in Ukraine. We are converting our steadfast commitment for Ukraine into capability that will help defend against Russia's barbaric attacks on civilians.
'Ukraine's frontline is the frontline for freedom and democracy, and we will stand with them for as long as it takes.'

Shares of Bill Holdings Inc. (BILL) jumped on Tuesday, hitting fresh 21-month highs, after reports that private equity firm TPG is nearing a take-private deal for the fintech company.
According to a report from The Financial Times citing people familiar with the matter, a take-private deal for Bill is likely to be agreed in the coming days and will value the company at a premium. However, the talks could also collapse, or the timeline could shift, the report added.

BILL had a market cap of about $4.8 billion before the bounce on Tuesday. The stock has dropped around 80% over the past five years after going public in late 2019. At the time of writing, BILL stock was trading 12% higher, on track for its best day since February, if the gains hold.
Bill Holdings has faced mounting pressure in recent years as revenue growth cooled from the triple-digit rates seen shortly after its 2019 IPO to the mid-teens.
The slowdown, combined with ongoing profitability challenges and a sharp decline in the stock from its 2021 peaks, has drawn activist investors including Starboard Value, Elliott Management, and Barington Capital, who have pushed for cost cuts, board changes, and a strategic review. The company has responded with workforce reductions and a greater focus on efficiency, even as competition intensified.
Earlier this month, the company headquartered in San Jose, California, reported quarterly total revenue of $353.8 million, an increase of 13% year-over-year, and net income of $60.3 million, compared to a loss of $3 million in the corresponding quarter of the previous fiscal year.
The company added that it processed 38 million transactions in the quarter, marking a growth of 14%, and served over 475,000 businesses as of the end of the quarter.
The news of a deal for Bill Holdings comes after its industry peer PayPal received a takeover proposal from private equity firm Advent International and Stripe earlier this year, though it did not culminate in a deal.

articles.title_orig: US signed off on sales of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China in six months, House committee says
articles.title_zh: US signed off on sales of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China in six months, House committee says
articles.content_orig:
The administration of United States President Donald Trump approved exports of nearly 900,000 advanced AI chips made by Nvidia and AMD for Chinese companies from December 2025 through May 2026, the House Foreign Affairs Committee has said.
The Department of Commerce’s approvals covered exports of 879,000 chips, including 75,000 for Alibaba, 150,000 for Tencent, 43,000 for Baidu and 4,000 for BYD, the committee said on Thursday.
Companies had sought permission to ship 3.4 million of them to China during the period, committee documents show.
The unusual release of chip export licensing data comes as the Trump administration faces heightened scrutiny following revelations about former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy , which fuelled renewed calls for a tougher stance against Chinese technology threats.
All four of the Chinese companies highlighted in the committee report are on the Pentagon’s list of alleged Chinese military-backed companies.
The committee chair, Brian Mast, has “exercised his authorities under the Export Control Reform Act to publicly reveal export control license application information regarding NVIDIA and AMD’s AI chip licenses for the People’s Republic of China”, the committee said in a statement. It was not immediately clear how many of the approvals resulted in actual China-bound shipments of the chips, which included Nvidia’s H200 and AMD’s equivalent MI325X.
News surrounding Huang has turned a spotlight on instances of Nvidia AI chips being smuggled to China that went unpunished, dialling up pressure on the Trump administration to crack down on Chinese tech threats.
“The fact that over 30 percent of the AI chips sent to China were shipped to companies that the Department of War has designated as Chinese military companies is astonishing, and calls into question whether Commerce conducted any serious national security review before approving these licenses,” said Chris McGuire, a former US official and expert on the US-China technology battle.
Nvidia said in a statement that the approvals were “subject to strict conditions and limited volumes”. It added that “despite receiving some licenses, we have since stopped shipping H200s to China”.
AMD did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Former US President Joe Biden had restricted Chinese access to the prized chips over fears that they would supercharge China’s military and erode the US lead in artificial intelligence.
But Trump in December gave the green light for Nvidia to ship its H200 chip to China, rolling back Biden-era restrictions and drawing fierce criticism from China hawks across the US political spectrum.
Nvidia’s stock ended the day down 3.3 percent, while AMD slumped 7.7 percent and the broader Nasdaq and S&P 500 were down 2.2 percent and 1.8 percent, respectively.

articles.title_orig: Trump, Xi, Putin sit down for a rare meeting in China
articles.title_zh: Trump, Xi, Putin sit down for a rare meeting in China
articles.content_orig:
President Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin sat down together in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday in a rare face-to-face encounter for the leaders of three of the world's most powerful countries, but there appeared to be little concrete to show for the meeting in terms of resolving any of the crises facing the world.
The leaders offered a joint statement after their roughly hour-and-a-half-long meeting. Mr. Trump immediately left for his return flight to the U.S. without speaking to journalists on the ground. On the flight home, the president said on social media he will hold a press conference at noon on Friday to discuss the trip.
The presidents discussed Russia's ongoing war in Ukraine , which Mr. Trump has wanted to bring to a negotiated end. But the only significant statement on the conflict came after the meeting from Putin, who ruled out any direct negotiations with Ukraine, citing a major strike earlier this week by Ukrainian forces on a key bridge in Russian-held Crimea.
Putin's senior aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters after the meeting that the atmosphere had been good, and the Kremlin quickly released what it called a joint statement from all three leaders characterizing the talks. The White House later provided the same statement.
The three men "exchanged views in detail on the current international situation and reaffirmed their commitment to maintaining strategic stability and international security," the readout said, adding that as permanent members of the United Nations Security Council, they had "reaffirmed their commitment to reforming the UN so that it can more effectively respond to global challenges and fulfill its fundamental mission in the area of international peace and security."
They also committed to increasing gas and oil production "for the benefit of all countries," agreed on the "fundamental importance" of "the principle of state consent and respect for the immunities of state officials," and said the " International Criminal Court and other similar bodies should not abuse their powers."
Finally, the leaders "reaffirmed that there can be no winners in a nuclear war, and that it should never be unleashed."
The White House indicated that Mr. Trump might speak with reporters on Air Force One during the flight back to the U.S.
The Kremlin shared a short video on social media, via Russian state media, showing Xi accompanying Putin as they walked out of the meeting to Putin's waiting motorcade. Before they exit the building, Putin is seen shaking Xi's hand, thanking him for hosting the gathering and telling him, according to Russian state media, that nobody had expected it to go so well.
Before the meeting, Mr. Trump met separately with Putin on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, and then with Xi.
"We've had a great relationship for many years," Mr. Trump said, standing alongside his Russian counterpart. "I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start."
As Mr. Trump approached Putin for a handshake, he said, "Who is that?" before laughing and saying, "He's my friend."
Democratic Sen. Tim Kaine, who sits on the Committee on Foreign Relations, said the image of Mr. Trump standing with Xi and Putin was concerning.
"Some of the pictures troubled me, seeing the president stand with Putin and Xi, rather than seeing the president stand with the leaders of the global democracies," Kaine said. "When I saw them, it turned my stomach a bit, and particularly President Trump's declaration that Vladimir Putin was a friend. Vladimir Putin is not a friend, and so you know he was either being insincere or he is deeply deluded if he thinks Vladimir Putin is a friend."
In a phone call with NBC reporter Gabe Gutierrez, Mr. Trump called the meeting a 12 on a scale of zero to 10.
Russia's TASS news agency said the war in Ukraine was the main topic discussed by the two leaders, and that Putin left the meeting in "an excellent mood."
After the trilateral talks Thursday, Putin told reporters that Ukraine and Europe were "not yet ready" to make the compromises necessary to resolve the war, according to Russian media.
"We will not negotiate after the attacks on the Crimean bridge," he declared, referring to this week's Ukrainian strike on the highly symbolic Kerch Bridge, which links Russia with Ukraine's Russian-occupied Crimean Peninsula.
Putin said Kyiv and Europe would eventually come to understand that it is better to make compromises than to face "realities."
Ukraine and its European partners have long feared that the White House appears willing to offer Putin too much — including the prospect of major energy deals — with no significant concessions from Russia  in return, while putting pressure on Kyiv to make major territorial concessions without any concrete security guarantees.
Mr. Trump then met for about an hour with Xi ahead of the three-way meeting. As the Trump-Xi session began, Xi told Mr. Trump relations between China and the United States were "stable and improved."
Mr. Trump told reporters he had spoken with Xi for two hours on Wednesday, with trade and tariffs being the main topics. He also said he would be asking China to "do some more" for American farmers, because China has an "insatiable appetite."
Mr. Trump said previously that he planned to talk about denuclearization with his fellow leaders. Russia and the United States are by far the world's largest holders of nuclear weapons , with stockpiles estimated at well over 5,000 warheads, while China is believed to be a distant third, with about 600 weapons.
Putin has made denuclearization a key talking point for decades, but both he and Mr. Trump have allowed previous treaties intended to limit nuclear proliferation to lapse in recent years. China, which has been building up its nuclear program , ruled out taking part in any denuclearization talks with the U.S. and Russia as recently as last year .
China's state-run Xinhua news agency quoted Xi , however, as saying ahead of the trilateral meeting on Thursday that nuclear weapons were a "sword of Damocles hanging over humanity," and calling for them to be "completely banned and completely destroyed, leading to a world free of nuclear weapons."
The Kremlin said in its readout of the three-way meeting that it would "continue dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons" with China and the U.S.
A range of other global challenges lingered in the background of the trilateral meeting, including the war in Iran and tension over trade and artificial intelligence .
The summit took place in the capital of the Chinese tech industry, a sector that has drawn intense scrutiny in recent weeks amid worries that advanced U.S. computer chips are surreptitiously reaching China. The scandal was sparked by allegations that now-former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a businesswoman and suspected Chinese intelligence asset, Alice Huang , whose company is accused of diverting Nvidia's coveted AI chips to China. Beijing has dismissed claims that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy as "groundless speculation" and "nothing more than an attempt to smear China."
Mr. Trump — an ally of Jensen Huang's — had previously told reporters he may bring up the businesswoman during his meetings in China, though he said, "I don't know that she is a spy." Her firm, Megaspeed , is under Justice Department investigation. It has denied wrongdoing.
Shortly after the concerns about Jensen Huang surfaced, the Trump administration issued a new rule aimed at curbing China and other countries' ability to remotely access advanced AI chips. China and the U.S. have also discussed broader AI policy issues in recent months, including setting up a communication channel to share information when AI systems go haywire.
Mr. Trump brought up AI during a speech at the APEC forum earlier in the day, vowing to block any "globalist regulation" of artificial int

articles.title_orig: Men guilty of abusing Joanne Young, who was drugged and advertised for sex by husband
articles.title_zh: Men guilty of abusing Joanne Young, who was drugged and advertised for sex by husband
articles.content_orig:
A woman who was drugged, raped and advertised for sex online by her husband has said she will "never feel completely safe" after four men were found guilty of sexually abusing her, in the first trial of its kind in England.
Joanne Young, who has waived her right to anonymity, said: "The person I trusted most in the world betrayed me in the most horrific way."
Philip Young, 50, had already pleaded guilty to multiple charges of drugging and raping his wife over a 13-year period at their home in Swindon, Wiltshire. He invited men via websites and apps such as Craigslist, Grindr and Fab Swingers to the couple's home without her knowledge.
On Thursday, Norman Macksoni, 48, Richard Wilkins, 62, Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, and Mohammed Hassan, 38, were found guilty of multiple sexual offences by a jury at Winchester Crown Court. Wilkins and Macksoni were each found guilty of one count of rape.
Joanne Young, who divorced Philip Young last year, said the abuse had "cost me my life as I knew it."
On the steps outside the court, she said: "What happened to me was not the act of one man alone, others were invited to take part and they chose to."
Joanne Young said the crimes committed against her had resulted in "a devastating impact on the lives of myself and my children".
She said: "I live with a pain that is hard to put into words and this is something that will affect our lives forever. It is terrifying that this could happen to anyone.
"What I have been through means I now never feel completely safe and while it can now be hard for me to leave the house, this horrific abuse showed me that home offered no protection either, even though at the time I believed I was safe."
She said the verdicts were significant "more broadly for women and girls who have been abused by men," sending the message "that you can be believed and understood".
She urged the government to look at the law of consent "as a priority" so that women were "properly protected in the future", adding her case had raised "serious questions".
Judge Mr Justice Saini had asked for calm as the verdicts were read out, with Joanne Young sitting in the public gallery surrounded by her family, her hands clasped over her mouth.
She gasped as the first guilty verdicts were read out against Connor Sanderson-Doyle, who dropped his head as he was convicted of one count of sexual assault by touching and one count of sexual assault by penetration.
The jury of eight men and four women also convicted Wilkins of one count of assault by penetration.
Hassan was found guilty of one count of sexual assault by touching.
A sixth defendant, Dean Hamilton, 47, of Street, in Somerset, admitted one charge of assault by penetration, two of sexual assault and one of rape at an earlier court hearing in February.
The judge commended Joanne Young and said she had shown "amazing bravery through these proceedings".
One police officer could also be seen sobbing as they left the court.
As all defendants were led from the courtroom after being told by the judge to expect lengthy jail terms when they are sentenced on 21 and 22 December, Joanne Young's family could be seen hugging.
Philip Young - who served as a Conservative Swindon borough councillor between 2007 and 2010 - drugged and raped his wife over 13 years and invited the men to have sex with her without her consent.
He pleaded guilty at an earlier court hearing to 56 charges made up of 14 counts of voyeurism, 11 of rape, 11 of administering a substance with intent, seven of assault by penetration, four of sexual assault and one of publishing obscene articles in relation to his wife.
James Foster, specialist Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) prosecutor, said: "This is the first time in the UK that a jury have convicted or been asked to consider a case of organised drug-facilitated sexual abuse, which has been organised by the husband."
The crimes of the former Tory councillor emerged after the highly publicised case in France of Gisèle Pelicot, whose husband, Dominique Pelicot, drugged and raped her and invited 50 other men to abuse her. Gisèle Pelicot also waived her right to anonymity in that trial.
Her husband was jailed for 20 years in France in 2024 and all the defendants were found guilty of at least one charge.
Police and prosecutors building the case against Philip Young sought the expertise of the French investigators to assist them in bringing him to justice.
Detectives discovered that Philip Young, whose most recent address was in Enfield, north London, had taken 480 intimate images and videos of his wife on 200 occasions and posted images online on at least 500 occasions – with the vast majority of these taken at the family home in Swindon.
The trial of the four defendants heard the investigation into Philip Young had begun after police were alerted to the fact he had uploaded extreme pornographic images to the internet in 2023.
Wiltshire Police said it was still looking for another man wanted in connection with alleged sex offences against Joanne Young.
They described him as being of "a large build, hairy, with scarring on the back of his head, prominent lips, short or shaved hair, and a distinctive tattoo on the left side of his chest".
Wiltshire Police added the extent of drug-rape offences was unknown because victims might not know they had been targeted.
A police spokesperson said: "While cases involving organised drug-facilitated sexual assault remain relatively rare compared to other forms of sexual offending, intelligence and other recent cases would suggest this may be a significantly under-reported crime type.
"Victims are often unaware they have been drugged, may have fragmented memories of events, or may initially attribute symptoms to alcohol consumption.
"These factors make detection and reporting particularly challenging."

articles.title_orig: Amazon fights the Delivery Protection Act with homepage banner, in-app pop-up
articles.title_zh: Amazon fights the Delivery Protection Act with homepage banner, in-app pop-up
articles.content_orig:
In an unprecedented move, Amazon is using its app and website to try to convince shoppers to not support a New York City bill.
When I log into Amazon today, I’m met with a vertical banner that reads: “ATTENTION NYC Council could add up to $5 per order” with a button that says “Act now.”
I also saw a smaller version of the notice on an order confirmation page on Amazon’s website. The message is delivered as a pop-up for users of the Amazon app, Bloomberg reported. Amazon hasn’t specified whether the messaging targets NYC residents based on addresses saved in their Amazon account or uses other techniques, such as device location services, but I only see the banner if I’m logged into Amazon.
Amazon is referring to Introduction 0518-2026 ( 518 ), also known as the Delivery Protection Act. If passed, it would require Amazon to directly employ the third-party delivery contractors that it uses.
Clicking on “Act now” on Amazon’s homepage or in the app brings up a page that gives shoppers a way to contact their NYC Council member and further states:
Right now, Amazon works with a network of small delivery businesses that are deeply embedded in your communities. If this legislation passes, we’d no longer be able to work with them, and we’d be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city. That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees.
It’s not unusual for Amazon to take a stance on political matters, and it has publicly opposed the Delivery Protection Act since April . What is new is Amazon using its online marketplace to push a political view. It’s uncommon to see a pop-up about legislation when visiting a shopping website.
The messaging suggests that Amazon is concerned about the potential impact the proposed law would have on its costs. Besides Amazon, the bill targets any company with last-mile delivery facilities in NYC, like FedEx and DoorDash.
It also raises questions about the potential impact on shoppers should Amazon expand its use of its e-commerce platform for additional political messaging. The pop-up launched today impacts only NYC residents but sets a precedent for Amazon to sway political views on other issues. Amazon has made similar moves internally, including reportedly using an app for its employees to campaign against unionizing. But the new pop-up shows Amazon extending that strategy directly to its users.
Given Amazon’s considerable influence in commerce, other companies could copy its actions. Uber and Lyft have previously done so, CNBC reports .
Finally, there’s the question of whether Amazon is fairly depicting the situations surrounding the bill. Notable supporters of the Delivery Protection Act include NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the Amazon division of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters. Using a platform with massive reach to communicate only one side of an ongoing debate could lead to misinformation and a skewed public perception.
The Delivery Protection Act is currently stalled in the City Council’s Committee on Consumer and Worker Protection. The last hearing on the bill was in April. A committee vote on whether to advance the act to the full City Council hasn’t been set.

articles.title_orig: Leaders of China, Russia, US praise trilateral summit as 'success'
articles.title_zh: Leaders of China, Russia, US praise trilateral summit as 'success'
articles.content_orig:
Xi, Putin and Trump outline priorities that include UN reform, boosting oil supplies and ‘protection of diplomatic immunity’
China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants.
The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it said was the protection of diplomatic immunity.
The statement affirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought”, but stopped short of suggesting the beginnings of a framework for denuclearisation.
The meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump has dominated the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit this week, with China, the host, promising it would be “groundbreaking”.
“We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”
Putin told a press conference later that the three men had had a “free discussion” and now had a “mutual understanding”.
Some had hopes that the talks, which lasted about one hour and 20 minutes, could be used to discuss reductions in arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers. Beijing has previously rebuffed Trump’s advances to join such talks, pointing to the larger US and Russian stockpiles. On Thursday, though, Xi called for nuclear weapons to “be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of [them]”.
The language of the declaration around nuclear war is the same as that previously issued by the five permanent members of the UN security council, which includes France and the UK.
“The real test will be whether the three countries follow through on their stated commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and preventing nuclear proliferation,” said Patricia Kim, an expert on Chinese foreign policy at the Brookings Institution, a US thinktank. Even the suggestion that China would engage was significant, said Yun Sun, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center.
Analysts had said that the meeting’s primary significance was in its optics. “Overall, very little of substance seems to have been accomplished … This summit appears to have been all about the symbolism and prestige value,” said Prof William Hurst, from the University of Cambridge’s Centre for Geopolitics. Putin pushed back at the suggestion the summit had just been a photo-op. “It is a serious collaborative work,” he said.
In the declaration, the men “committed themselves to maintaining strategic stability and international security”.
First among their concerns was “promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges”. Sun said this was a favourite topic of China’s and showed that Beijing was “flexing its diplomatic muscles”. She said: “It is able to set the agenda and the deliverables according to its priorities … and make other great powers accept them.”
The declaration also agreed that “the international criminal court [ICC] and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction”. Putin is subject to an ICC arrest warrant and so the clause added to the perception that he has done well from the summit. Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Russian president has been treated as an international pariah by Kyiv’s allies and he has not been to an Apec summit in years.
Hurst said: “This was no Yalta moment, but it was certainly a solid public demonstration of Russia’s (and Putin’s) continuing relevance and power. It’s yet another example of Putin playing a poor hand to maximum effect.”
Xi, his status as a global power broker now assured, began the morning by addressing Apec leaders, reiterating the themes of trade openness and innovation he has emphasised throughout the summit. However, Apec affairs appeared to take a back seat for most of the day, with business dominating the discussions. For all the camaraderie on display, relations are complex. Russia is under US sanctions over the Ukraine war, while China and the US spent much of the last year engaged in an escalating tit-for-tat trade war before Trump and Xi called a truce .
Trump and Putin earlier held a separate meeting – their first since August 2025 – where the US president called his Russian counterpart his “friend”.
European allies meeting in Berlin to show their support for Ukraine expressed indignation at the cosy optics. “Mr Putin is not our friend and ⁠will never be,” the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, said in a rejoinder to Trump. The Danish prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, said she found it “very incomprehensible” that a US ​president would want to sit down with Putin.
The peace declaration in Shenzhen said the three countries planned “to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”. That was important, said Shan Guo from Hutong Research, a Shanghai-based advisory firm, but “now let’s see if the US will lift sanctions”.
Trump and Xi then held their third bilateral of this year. Xi said the US-China relationship was “generally stable and positive”, according to state media. But he cautioned Washington over Taiwan, saying the US “must keep doing the right thing to avoid major setbacks in US-China relations”.
Another watched-for topic lacking detailed findings was that of AI. Xi said the two countries should “enhance communication and coordination to guard against security risks … and ensure that AI remains under human control at all times”.
Ultimately, the lack of breakthroughs might suit China, which has no appetite to move beyond the role of convener, said Kim. “Beijing has little interest in taking on the diplomatic risks of brokering an actual peace agreement in Ukraine or resolving the conflict with Iran. That would entangle China in conflicts it would rather avoid,” she said.

articles.title_orig: Social Security raise: What’s left after the Medicare premium hike?
articles.title_zh: Social Security raise: What’s left after the Medicare premium hike?
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
An increase in older Americans’ Medicare Part B premium is set to eat into the larger Social Security payments they are expected to receive next year.
Recipients will get a 3.6 percent boost to their Social Security checks starting in January, bringing their average monthly payments to $2,170.
While an extra $75 a month helps relieve some of the financial strain that many Americans are facing , especially for seniors on a fixed income, not all will see all the money thanks to a Medicare Part B premium hike.
Older Americans with Medicare Part B — which covers doctor’s visits, outpatient hospital services, and other health services not covered by Medicare Part A — will see their monthly premiums increase next year by $6.50 to $209.40.
The federal government’s Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services said the premium is largely due to expected increases in health spending.
Most Part B enrollees have their premium taken out of their Social Security payments, leaving them with less disposable income for housing, food and other basic necessities, AARP explains.
The 3.6 percent Cost of Living Adjustment for next year was determined by looking at the federal government’s Consumer Price Index from the third quarter of 2025 through the third quarter of 2026.
Costs have continued to rise, with food prices up 0.5 percent, energy prices up 0.7 percent, and the price for all other items up 0.3 percent in October from September, according to the latest Consumer Price Index.
Notably, the $2,170 monthly check is an average estimate of Social Security benefits. Many older Americans receive much smaller checks, meaning if they have their Medicare Part B premium withheld, they are left with even less money, NewsNation reports.
Healthcare will be a major part of Democrats’ agenda after they take control of the House and Senate in January.
Democratic lawmakers will likely try to reinstate the COVID-era Affordable Care Act subsidies to lower premiums and reverse President Donald Trump’s Medicaid cuts.
But Senate Democrats are almost certain to run into problems with the filibuster, and even if they get legislation passed, it will have to be signed by Trump, who has made clear that he’s not afraid to use his veto power .

articles.title_orig: Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan Customer Data Leaked by Hackers
articles.title_zh: Visa, Mastercard and JPMorgan Customer Data Leaked by Hackers
articles.content_orig:
Payment services were unaffected, the companies said.
JPMorganChase said Thursday morning that "third parties who provide services" to the banking giant "were the target of a cyberattack."
"Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses," the statement continued.
"There is no disruption to our services," according to the statement.
JPMorganChase, the largest U.S. bank, did not disclose when the cyberattack occurred or name the third-party companies that were targeted.
"Where appropriate, we will contact affected customers directly and offer support, including complimentary credit monitoring," the company said in its statement.
JPMorganChase said on Monday that it experienced technical issues that triggered online delays across several major U.S. banks and blamed the outage on a "software bug." The company said Thursday that it found "no connection to service disruptions some customers experienced earlier this week" regarding the third-party provider data breach.
Mastercard also reported on Thursday that one of its third-party providers was hacked, while Visa said earlier this week that it was aware that one of its third-party providers experienced a data breach.
"They are associated with an incident involving a third-party service provider in Asia Pacific," Visa said in its statement. "Visa’s systems were not involved and were not impacted. No payments data such as card numbers were affected."
"We were recently informed of an incident at a third-party provider that resulted in the exposure of [a] limited amount of email addresses – non-payments information – from a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program," Mastercard said in its statement Thursday.
"There is no impact to the Mastercard payment network or the ability for people to use their cards," Mastercard further said. "At this time, the exposure has been contained, and our teams are working with the provider to support the impacted cardholders as needed."
There have been several recent tech outages across the nation that affected air travel, email and hotel reservations, and even slowed classified internal communications at the National Security Agency.
Top Trump administration officials continued this week to insist that there is no evidence that those outages were the result of cyberattacks.

articles.title_orig: Appeals court grants Trump request to halt order restoring Venezuelan TPS
articles.title_zh: Appeals court grants Trump request to halt order restoring Venezuelan TPS
articles.content_orig:
A United States appeals court has allowed the administration of President Donald Trump to move forward for now with the removal of deportation protections for Venezuelans .
The ruling on Wednesday cancels out a previous order by a lower-court judge that required the government to restore the Temporary Protected Status (TPS) of Venezuelans, which shields recipients against deportation.
The effort to end the TPS protections has proceeded despite humanitarian concerns .
Since taking office for a second term, Trump has sought to carry out what he calls the largest deportation effort in US history. Part of that agenda has been to roll back programmes like TPS.
But in September 2025, US District Judge Edward Chen blocked the expiration of TPS protections for Venezuelans, arguing that deporting those individuals would put them in harm’s way.
He also ruled that the Trump administration had overstepped its authority by seeking to shorten TPS extensions granted under the preceding president, Joe Biden. Such decisions, Chen added, needed to be taken with “careful study and analysis”.
Some 600,000 Venezuelans in the US were protected under TPS programmes.
The Supreme Court paused Chen’s ruling in October 2025. But that pause expired this month, and Chen’s order was set to take effect on Friday.
On Wednesday, the Trump administration filed an emergency request to the Supreme Court to extend the pause before Thursday’s appeals court ruling.
The appeals court’s decision does not nix the ongoing legal challenges to Trump’s efforts to revoke TPS extensions. But it allows the administration to suspend deportation protections while the challenges make their way through court.
The Trump administration has sought to strip large numbers of immigrants of their legal protections in a bid to render them deportable. Other programmes, like humanitarian parole, have also come under the administration’s scrutiny.
TPS allows foreign nationals already in the US to remain while conditions in their home countries are too dangerous or unstable to return to.
Humanitarian parole, meanwhile, allows people outside the US to come in on a temporary basis, often to escape similarly perilous conditions.
The Trump administration has argued that TPS designations are meant to be temporary — and that previous presidencies extended such protections without cause.
It has also maintained that conditions have improved in places like Venezuela, where a US military action on January 3 resulted in the abduction of President Nicolas Maduro.
Human rights advocates, however, have noted that Maduro’s government remains largely intact. That leadership has been accused of abuses ranging from arbitrary imprisonment to the torture of political dissidents.
The US Department of State currently warns against travel to Venezuela, citing issues such as crime, kidnapping and poor health infrastructure.

articles.title_zh: Apple Is Working on AI Agent for Device Control, Apps, Browsing and Coding
articles.content_orig:
Apple’s job listing describes an AI agent that can browse the web, work across apps, and call services.
Apple’s job listing describes an AI agent that can browse the web, work across apps, and call services.
Apple is working on its own AI agent that can perform a range of tasks for you, including browsing the web, working across apps, writing code, and calling services. That’s according to a job listing spotted by Bloomberg , which says Apple is looking for an engineer to lead the creation of an agentic AI assistant.
An AI agent from Apple would put the iPhone maker in the running to compete with the likes of Meta’s Muse , OpenAI’s Dots , Anthropic’s Duet , and Google’s Tasks . Muse, ChatGPT, and Perplexity can already take control of a computer through their Mac apps, while Google just started letting Gemini do the same.
Apple began rolling out its AI-upgraded Siri in September, which you can use to ask questions about what’s on your screen, as well as perform actions across apps. It looks like Apple is planning to give Siri more agentic capabilities , as a report from Bloomberg suggests the company could add the ability to rotate and crop images in Photos, or organize Safari tabs. This lines up with the company’s new job listing, which says the engineer will work closely with teams across its Siri, UI Frameworks, and Apple Foundation Models divisions.
“People already do their most valuable work by moving fluidly between tools: a browser, a document, a terminal, an editor, a service,” the job listing says. “We’re building AI agents that can do the same… These agents plan and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, and they can coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way.”
With its upcoming iOS 27.3 update , Apple is also giving developers the ability to integrate Siri AI into “all apps.” This is rolling out as part of a Developer Preview and will eventually allow Siri to perform tasks across a wider range of apps.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic becomes most valuable AI firm in first-of-its kind IPO
articles.title_zh: Anthropic becomes most valuable AI firm in first-of-its kind IPO
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic has become one of the most valuable public companies in the world after its shares began trading on the public stock market, taking its valuation to roughly $1.76 trillion.
The artificial intelligence (AI) company's Thursday debut on the Nasdaq stock exchange was a crucial test for the industry, given the huge amount of money being poured into advancing the technology.
Anthropic's shares flew past its allocation price of $83 per share , showing there is plenty of excitement around AI.
Yet the company, which is behind AI chatbot Claude, will remain under intense scrutiny in the months ahead to answer the key question surrounding AI: is it all worth it?
In just a few hours of trading, Anthropic's stock seemed to show that investors remain uncertain of where exactly AI is heading. The share price rose immediately to $111.5, sending the company's market value to almost $2 trillion, before falling by the end of the day, with shares hitting $97.
Some investors said Anthropic's debut seemed to be a success, as shares rose roughly 17% during the day, but the broader tech market did not perform as well.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index closed down nearly 2.3%. Stocks fell in the largest tech firms, including Google's parent company Alphabet (down 3%) and Amazon (down 3.9%).
The build-out happening around this era of AI is among the most expensive endeavours in the history of technology, with more than $1 trillion being spent in the last year alone by a handful of major tech companies.
The speed at which investment has grown has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble.
"Bubbles don't burst on the day of the largest deal," Richard Whittle, an economist with the University of Salford said. "They burst later, if the positive future becomes suspect."
While the basics of the technology have been around for decades, the more recent advent of more powerful computers and related components have allowed the processing of more data than ever.
The result has been AI chatbots that simulate human speech and operate more quickly tasks like software coding, digital image generation, and searching the internet.
It represents a new way of using computers that has led to the rapid rise of Anthropic, which started just five years ago and is best known as the maker of the popular AI chatbot Claude.
As the first purely AI company to go public, Anthropic will almost certainly see significant swings in price on the stock market going forward, according to Ben Barringer, who leads technology research at Quilter Cheviot.
The "initial exuberance" will wear off, Barringer said, pointing to what happened with SpaceX earlier this year.
That company, led by Elon Musk, saw shares jump by about 10% on the first day of trading, taking the company to a record-breaking valuation of $2.2 trillion.
Within a month shares had fallen below their debut price, and have mostly fallen further since.
Most tech companies see their shares fall after hitting the stock market, often after reporting quarterly results for the first time.
But many such companies, including Meta, Amazon and Google, have gone on to become the largest and most profitable corporations in the world.
With Anthropic, investors are not only looking at a notable tech company with a major valuation, and a potentially big future in business, but a company that is the first of its kind on the stock market.
"There's no obvious peer to compare it to," Neil Wilson, an investor strategist at Saxo UK, said.
So, as individual investors and even researchers and investors at large funds ask themselves if Anthropic is really worth $1.5 trillion, or even more, there will be few answers available.
"We'll have a stab at it," Wilson said. "I don't think anyone really knows."
A few things will likely impact the company's success on the stock market in the near-term.
One of those things is the prospect of new laws governing the use of AI tools. In the US, where Anthropic is based, Democrats will be in many more positions of power come 2027, and several politicians have already said they will be looking to ensure AI tools are safe and have some guardrails attached.
On Thursday, the same day Anthropic went public, a bipartisan group of lawmakers formed the House AI Safety and Innovation Caucus, which will work specifically on AI regulation and safety considerations.
A significant driver of this kind of scrutiny is Anthropic itself. Company executives, including co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei, have been outspoken in their purported fears that future AI tools will become so capable they will outsmart humans, to the point where extinction is possible.
Anthropic has always put itself forward in public as an AI company that takes the safety of its technology very seriously.
Daniela Amodei, Anthropic's president and sister of Dario Amodei, boasted on Thursday that the company "had an AI safety team before we launched our first product".
"AI carries real risks," she added.
Despite the company's claims that the technology it is building at a rapid pace could be dangerous, Anthropic has made one of the quickest trips from start-up to IPO in history.

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: U.N. Court Rules Myanmar Committed Genocide Against Rohingya
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: U.N. Court Rules Myanmar Committed Genocide Against Rohingya
articles.content_orig:
In a landmark verdict, the United Nations’ top court has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Muslim minority Rohingya population in a brutal 2017 military crackdown that drove more than 730,000 Rohingya to flee to neighbouring Bangladesh.
The ruling at the International Court of Justice (ICJ) at The Hague on Thursday is the first time a state has been found responsible for genocide at the court, and only the fourth time since the Nazi Holocaust that an international court ruled that the crime had been committed.
ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said the court, in a 9-6 decision, found that Myanmar “has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine state, in violation of its obligations under the Genocide Convention”.
Evidence showed Myanmar forces killed at least 10,000 Rohingya people, Iwasawa said during a three-hour readout of the verdict.
“The Court finds that Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated widespread acts of sexual violence, as well as acts of extreme violence against children, and attacked fleeing Rohingya as they sought to flee in large numbers to Bangladesh,” he said.
In the specific cases that he referred to, Iwasawa said Myanmar had acted with “genocidal intent”.
The Special Advisory Council for Myanmar welcomed the judgement but stressed that the decision must lead to concrete accountability measures and reparations for victims.
Founding member Yanghee Lee said in a statement that it was a “deeply emotional day for all Rohingya people”, adding that “justice has been decided, but not yet delivered”.
“For decades, the Burmese military tried to erase our identity, deny our existence, and dismiss our suffering,” said Wai Wai Nu, executive director of the Women’s Peace Network and a former political prisoner.
“By finding that Myanmar committed genocide, ordering a guarantee of non-repetition, and ordering restitution and compensation, the world’s highest court has permanently shattered that state-sponsored lie,” she said.
Gambia, which brought the case to the court, called the ruling “a historic day for international justice” and urged Myanmar to comply “fully and without delay”.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the United Kingdom would expel Myanmar’s defence attache and called for an urgent UN Security Council session to discuss the judgement.
Myanmar claimed its crackdown was in response to attacks on police posts by fighters from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA).
The ICJ said that the “only reasonable inference” from evidence of widespread atrocities by Myanmar security forces is that they had the intent to destroy a “substantial part” of the Rohingya minority.
It said Myanmar should have known that there was a risk of genocide when armed civilians participated in the military campaign. “Myanmar thus violated its obligation to prevent genocide,” it added.
Myanmar is now obliged to provide reparations and restitution “as a result of Myanmar’s wrongful acts”, Iwasawa said.
The court said appropriate restitution by Myanmar would include facilitating the safe and voluntary return of Rohingya; returning or replacing all collective property damaged; facilitating the search for the disappeared and ensuring proper burials; providing for the physical and psychological rehabilitation of those mentally injured; and ensuring the population’s protection from persecution.
Reporting from the Hague, Al Jazeera’s Step Vaessen said the verdict is “extremely important for the Rohingya”.
“They’ve been waiting for 10 years for any kind of justice, but it’s also important for the whole international community because genocide is such a difficult act to prove.”
The hardest part of any genocide case is proving specific intent to destroy a group in whole or in part – an extremely high bar – said Toby Cadman, an international human rights lawyer. He noted that the ICJ had never before ruled that a state has specific intent to commit genocide.
“The court is guided by the genocide convention and what the genocide convention states, and it is a high threshold,” Cadman told Al Jazeera.
Human rights organisations welcomed the judgement. “We hope this ruling marks the beginning of a long overdue process of accountability in Myanmar,” Amnesty International said in a statement. It added that all crimes under international law “must be effectively investigated and those suspected of responsibility brought to justice”.
Cadman said that the situation does not come to an end with the ICJ’s ruling and a lot will depend on what comes next. This includes whether the issue goes before the UN Security Council and whether there are sanctions, or other remedies that the court can order to ensure it is enforced.
More than 1.3 million Rohingya remain displaced across South and Southeast Asia, including 1.2 million in sprawling refugee camps in Cox’s Bazar in Bangladesh, according to the UN. Conflict, shrinking humanitarian aid and dangerous sea crossings continue to leave many members of the community displaced and vulnerable.

articles.title_orig: Trump says no rush on Iran decision, looks to next year
articles.title_zh: Trump says no rush on Iran decision, looks to next year
articles.content_orig:
Iran's foreign ministry rejected President Trump's accusations the country is developing chemical or biological weapons and compared the situation to then-Secretary of State Colin Powell asserting Iraq had weapons of mass destruction.
"After the grand narrative of the 'Iranian nuclear threat,' U.S. officials are now claiming that there are indications Iran is developing biological or chemical weapons!" Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei said in a post on X . "The allegations keep changing, but the underlying narrative remains disturbingly familiar. Once again, the world is apparently expected to suffer a bout of collective amnesia."
Baqaei raised the specter of the U.S. invasion of Iraq in 2003 over alleged development of weapons of mass destruction by Saddam Hussein's government and asked why Americans would fall for it again.
"Do American officials really expect the world to forget Colin Powell's infamous appearance before the U.N. Security Council in 2003, when he held up a small vial as a visual representation of the alleged threat posed by Iraq's weapons of mass destruction?" the spokesperson said. "That moment has since become an enduring symbol of one of the most consequential intelligence failures and political deceptions in modern history."
He added, "And now we find ourselves facing ominous new allegations and a narrative that appears to be following the same fraudulent script."
Mr. Trump on Wednesday had claimed there was an "indication" Iran was looking to develop chemical or biological weapons because the U.S. had "shut them out" of obtaining nuclear weapons.
"They're looking at gases, looking at bio, because we've shut them out with the nuclear," Mr. Trump told a Fox reporter in Shenzhen, China.
The Senate rejected a House-adopted resolution aimed at reining in President Trump's ability to strike Iran, losing Republican support despite frustration with the war following the party's losses in the midterm elections.
In a 48 to 51 vote, three Republicans — Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Rand Paul of Kentucky — joined all but one Senate Democrat — Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania — in support of the measure.
Thursday's vote marked the first time either chamber has weighed in on the war since the midterm elections, which dealt Republicans sweeping losses. Voters cited the war in Iran, and its toll on the economy, as among their top concerns.
The resolution would have directed the president "to remove United States Armed Forces from hostilities with Iran," but its impact would have been largely symbolic.
Iraqi forces will begin deploying on Friday in the main stronghold of the Iran-backed Kataeb Hezbollah group, state media reported, as Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi steps up efforts to rein in the faction.
Kataeb Hezbollah on Tuesday adopted a softer tone toward the U.S.-backed premier, with Iraqi sources saying a compromise was reached during a visit by Iranian commander Esmail Qaani.
Iraq has faced mounting U.S. pressure to curb Iran's influence and contain Tehran-backed armed groups — a difficult task in a country long caught between its two allies.
Tensions have grown between Zaidi and Kataeb Hezbollah since the U.S.-backed leader vowed to disarm Iran-backed groups that have long-targeted U.S. interests in the region — a longstanding American demand but a tall order for Baghdad.
This week, Zaidi gave Kataeb Hezbollah a deadline to withdraw from Jurf al-Sakher, also known as Jurf al-Nasr, which lies south of Baghdad, after the government said an investigative committee had confirmed oil smuggling in the area — a claim the armed group denied.
President Trump told Channel 12 News in Israel that he is in no hurry to make any decisions on the war with Iran, and could in fact wait until next year.
"I'm not rushing to make any decisions on Iran," Mr. Trump told Keshet 12's Barak Ravid, who spoke to the president as he returned from China. "We'll see what happens after the new year starts."
The story noted Mr. Trump could also change his mind, though.
The tone seems in line with his and Secretary of State Marco Rubio's comments from last week. Mr. Trump called new strikes "quite unlikely," while Rubio said new strikes weren't needed since the economic sanctions campaign was working so well.
In an interview with Fox News on Wednesday, Mr. Trump said he had no need to ask China or Russia for help with an Iran deal.
"They want to make a deal, so I don't need help," Mr. Trump told the network. "I mean, I'm not going to go in asking for help. And frankly, they've treated us very well. They haven't fired. They haven't put ships in the water."
The war against Iran has cost the U.S. military more than $48 billion since the conflict began in late February, a Pentagon official said Thursday.
"That number includes munitions, equipment replacement costs, and operational cost," Arthur Miller, the Pentagon's deputy comptroller, told lawmakers during a hearing on his nomination as assistant secretary of the Navy for financial management.
The figure does not include damage to U.S. bases in the Middle East, some of which have been hit hard by Iranian drone and missile attacks, nor does it take into account the harm to the global economy.
The update was the first since mid-October, when the war's cost was pegged at $47.1 billion, according to an estimate from the U.S. Central Command obtained by CBS News. The bulk of that price tag at the time was replacing used munitions at about $29 billion. Lost equipment, including planes and unmanned aircraft, accounted for about $6 billion.
Iran said Thursday that it will not accept "unconditional and unlimited cooperation" with inspectors from the United Nations' International Atomic Energy Agency while it is being bombed.
"We do not accept being targeted on the one hand and being asked in a demanding tone on the other to provide accurate information about our materials and facilities and to provide unlimited access to them," Reza Najafi, Iran's ambassador and permanent representative to the United Nations and international organizations in Vienna, said Thursday, according to Iran's semi-official ISNA news agency.
"While adhering to its obligations, Iran will not accept unconditional and unlimited cooperation with the Agency [IAEA] and will review each inspection request on a case-by-case basis, taking into account security conditions," he added.
The nuclear issue, including IAEA access to Iran's nuclear sites, has been a key sticking point in negotiations between Tehran and Washington.
President Trump has justified the war as a necessary action to prevent Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. Iran has always denied any nuclear weapons aspirations, but it has enriched uranium to near-weapons grade. The exact whereabouts and condition of that material, and the circumstances of many facilities themselves, have remained unclear since the U.S. and Israel launched a major attack on the sites in June 2025. Iran has refused IAEA access to its nuclear facilities since then.
Saudi Arabia has condemned Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen for targeting a skyscraper in the financial district of Riyadh, the kingdom's capital.
"The Ministry of Foreign Affairs expresses the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia's strong condemnation and denunciation of the continued terrorist attacks by the Houthi terrorist militia targeting civilian and economic facilities and civilian objects in the capital, Riyadh, and the resulting material damage to the King Abdullah Financial District," the ministry wrote in a post on X .
Earlier, Saudi Arabia's civil defense agency said the building was damaged in a Houthi strike but that there were no injuries.
The Iran-backed Houthis struck a tower in Riyadh's financial district on Thursday, causing damage but no injuries, Saudi authorities said.
