articles.title_orig: Trump China trip: Iran and Ukraine not in 'peace declaration' and more takeaways - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Trump China trip: Iran and Ukraine not in 'peace declaration' and more takeaways - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
Trump, Xi and Putin don't have much to say after their historic meeting.
President Donald Trump is headed back to Washington after a historic trilateral meeting with presidents Xi Jinping of China and Vladimir Putin of Russia -- the first-ever sitdown between the three global superpowers -- with no tangible diplomatic breakthroughs in hand.
Following their meeting, the three leaders released what was described as a symbolic four-point "peace declaration," focusing on reform at the United Nations, oil supply, nuclear risk reduction and opposition to what it called the International Criminal Court's "jurisdiction abuse."
ABC News has reached out to the ICC for comment.
The symbolic peace declaration made no mention of Russia's war with Ukraine, which is in its fifth year, or the war with Iran. Both Russia and China have faced accusations by U.S. and European officials of providing satellite imagery and broader intelligence support to Iran, accusations both countries have denied.
Trump left Shenzhen without taking questions from reporters after the meeting but announced in a post on his social media platform while traveling back to Washington that he would hold a news conference at the White House on Friday.
Here are takeaways from Trump's trip:
The three leaders affirmed their commitment that nuclear war should never be fought but announced no commitments to reduce their respective nuclear arsenals.
Trump had insisted nuclear arms control be a central topic of the summit.
"As the world's three largest nuclear powers by far, the United States, Russia, and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on Earth, and also to lessen the risk that those weapons will ever be used," Trump said in brief remarks ahead of the meeting. "The power is unbelievable, unthinkable."
“It’s not an ​easy thing to do -- give them up,” Trump said.
Trump also used the issue of nuclear proliferation to defend the U.S. war with Iran, repeating his assertion that Iran cannot obtain a nuclear weapon.
"It's also vital that we cooperate to combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world. That's what we're doing in Iran. We're not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon," he said.
In a joint statement released following the meeting, the three leaders said they had an "in-depth exchange of views on the current international situation" and "committed to maintaining strategic stability and international security."
Trump, Xi, and Putin said the three countries will conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons.
The “peace declaration” released after the meeting made no mention of Russia’s war in Ukraine or the U.S.-led war in Iran.
"We are going to be discussing the war between Russia and Ukraine, and we already have. President Putin and I have had a long discussion today for quite a while. That's what pretty much what the discussion was about, and I think things are happening," Trump said.
For his part, Putin briefly commented on his escalating war in Ukraine during opening remarks.
"Our countries have numerous shared interests in the settlement of regional conflicts, including obviously the conflict in Ukraine. We discussed this yesterday with the Chairman of the People's Republic of China and today at the initiative of the U.S. president, we devoted significant attention to this during our bilateral meeting," the Russian president said, speaking through a translator.
The leaders also declared they plan to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products "for the benefit of all nations" while also reaffirming the importance of the stable flow of energy.
The oil market has been roiled in the nine months of the U.S.'s war with Iran, with the critical waterway through which a fifth of the world’s oil supplies has transited under constant threat. Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy facilities have further exacerbated global energy flows.
There were no signs upon conclusion of their meeting that Trump secured any agreements from Xi or Putin to help solve the Iran conflict.
Trump also highlighted that the three would discuss the International Criminal Court, the international body that works to uphold international law and prosecute war crimes. The Trump administration has targeted the ICC and its judges with sanctions and has sharply criticized the body.
"In another area of potential cooperation between us, I'll be suggesting ways to protect our nation's sovereignty from rogue globalist organizations such as the International Criminal Court, which has gotten out of control, which I believe we all agree has really strayed far from beyond its jurisdiction," Trump said in his opening remarks.
As part of the peace declaration, the three heads of state "recognized that the principle of state consent and respect for immunities of State officials are of paramount importance, and concurred that the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction."

Boston's iconic CITGO sign is ready to shine again. After months of restoration that saw it temporarily removed from the city skyline, the Kenmore Square landmark will be relit on Thursday night.
Over the past decade , we've reported on the CITGO sign's place in Boston lore, the effort to protect it and the plans to restore and relocate it.
All of that led to this year's restoration and relocation effort , which was part of a Kenmore Square redevelopment project. It involved shifting the sign 30 feet higher and 120 feet to the east of its original location.
Thursday's public celebration of the project and relighting of the sign will be held at the Commonwealth Avenue Mall in Kenmore Square, from 6 to 8 p.m. Organizers plan to feature free musical performances by the Boston University Pep Band and the Berklee College of Music House Band and a relighting countdown.

articles.title_orig: Stocks plunge as investors take cover amid growing uncertainty
articles.title_zh: Stocks plunge as investors take cover amid growing uncertainty
articles.content_orig:
The Dow Jones Industrial Average plunged more than 1,100 points on Thursday, while other stock markets also slid, amid fears that the boom in artificial intelligence stocks may be deflating.
The Dow tumbled 1,101 points, or 2.2%, to close at 49,097, while the S&P 500 slipped 2%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index fell 2.3%.
The swoon in markets was broad, with more than 90% of S&P 500 stocks nosing down.
Wall Street analysts said no single catalyst accounted for the plunge, but rather pointed to ongoing concerns about the durability of financial markets that lean heavily on AI's financial prospects. Despite those concerns, Anthropic had a successful stock market debut, with its shares rising as much as 34% in Thursday trading after staging the biggest initial public offering in history.
"The slump has set off a scramble of headline searching as people scour the wires to find the most negative sounding news flash," Adam Crisafulli, an analyst at Vital Knowledge, said in a research note. "People just don't have much enthusiasm for this market, and rallies tend to bring out sellers instead of chasers (there is still a lot of hesitation when it comes to being long AI-linked names, especially picks-and-shovels, and the defensive stuff is quite extended after the recent rally)."
For weeks, investors have fretted about the financial strength of the AI sector amid concerns that the torrent of capital pouring into data centers may not deliver the productivity and profit growth companies are counting on.
More recently, investors were shaken by the resignation earlier this month of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang after the revelation that he had a relationship with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Some lawmakers have increased scrutiny of Nvidia's sales to China and to companies in southeast China, while the Commerce Department this week signaled it plans to tighten export controls on AI chips.
On Thursday, shares of AI-related stocks went from morning gains to afternoon losses. Micron Technology, whose sales of memory for computers have soared amid the AI boom, initially rallied 7.8% before swinging to a 1.8% loss. CoreWeave, a company that buys AI chips and rents access to them to customers via the cloud, went from a 10.5% morning gain to a 5.5% drop.
Nvidia erased an early gain of 4.7% and flipped to a loss of 2.7%. The chip company has been the face of the AI boom, and its stock has struggled with the worries that have been dogging the entire industry.
It wasn't only tech stocks that tumbled on Thursday. Williams-Sonoma dropped 15.3% after the company behind Pottery Barn and West Elm reported revenue for the latest quarter that was just below Wall Street's forecast.
Walmart sank 1.2% even though the retailing giant reported profit and revenue for the latest quarter that edged past analysts' expectations.
The Associated  Press contributed to this report.

Payment services were unaffected, the companies said.
JPMorganChase said Thursday morning that "third parties who provide services" to the banking giant "were the target of a cyberattack."
"Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses," the statement continued.
"There is no disruption to our services," according to the statement.
JPMorganChase, the largest U.S. bank, did not disclose when the cyberattack occurred or name the third-party companies that were targeted.
"Where appropriate, we will contact affected customers directly and offer support, including complimentary credit monitoring," the company said in its statement.
JPMorganChase said on Monday that it experienced technical issues that triggered online delays across several major U.S. banks and blamed the outage on a "software bug." The company said Thursday that it found "no connection to service disruptions some customers experienced earlier this week" regarding the third-party provider data breach.
Mastercard also reported on Thursday that one of its third-party providers was hacked, while Visa said earlier this week that it was aware that one of its third-party providers experienced a data breach.
"They are associated with an incident involving a third-party service provider in Asia Pacific," Visa said in its statement. "Visa’s systems were not involved and were not impacted. No payments data such as card numbers were affected."
"We were recently informed of an incident at a third-party provider that resulted in the exposure of [a] limited amount of email addresses – non-payments information – from a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program," Mastercard said in its statement Thursday.
"There is no impact to the Mastercard payment network or the ability for people to use their cards," Mastercard further said. "At this time, the exposure has been contained, and our teams are working with the provider to support the impacted cardholders as needed."
There have been several recent tech outages across the nation that affected air travel, email and hotel reservations, and even slowed classified internal communications at the National Security Agency.
Top Trump administration officials continued this week to insist that there is no evidence that those outages were the result of cyberattacks.

articles.title_orig: Gap names new Athleta CEO, lowers full-year guidance
articles.title_zh: Gap names new Athleta CEO, lowers full-year guidance
articles.content_orig:
Gap Inc. on Thursday announced Ashley Kechter will be the next president and CEO of its Athleta brand, effective Dec. 14.
Kechter comes to Gap from activewear retailer Vuori, where she was global president and oversaw the brand's global business strategy, marketing and financials. She was previously global brand president of Fabletics and began her career at Gap before that.
"I'm excited to return to Gap Inc. and partner with [Gap CEO Richard Dickson] and the team to strengthen our connection with customers and shape the brand's next chapter," Kechter said in a statement.
The announcement comes after Lululemon poached former Athleta CEO Maggie Gauger to be its chief product officer last month.
"Clearly, we're disappointed with Athleta's performance, and we recognize there's a lot of work ahead," Dickson told CNBC. "We had been in rebuild mode, but now we're really in turnaround mode."
Dickson said the company is focused on getting back to its fundamentals: fabrications, feature, form, function and fit. Dickson added that Kechter will be conducting a "comprehensive review" of the brand to reposition Athleta for future success.
While the execution of its strategy has thus far "fallen short," Dickson said this new approach will allow Athleta to fully realize its potential.
Gap also reported mixed fiscal third-quarter earnings on Thursday and posted flat overall comparable sales. Wall Street had been expecting a comparable sales increase of 1.3%, according to StreetAccount.
Net sales grew 2%, though demand softened in October and early November due to warmer weather, the company said. Store sales increased 1%, while online sales increased 3%.
Gap also said it's recorded a $420 million adjustment to cost of goods sold and a $21 million adjustment to interest income from tariff refunds so far this year.
The company lowered its full-year net sales outlook to be "roughly flat," down from previous guidance of up between 1% and 1.5%. Gap is also now expecting adjusted earnings per share of between $2.29 and $2.34, down from an earlier expectation of between $2.35 and $2.45 per share.
Dickson said in an interview that much of the lowered guidance was due to warmer weather in the first two weeks of the quarter, but he said Gap is expecting "meaningful acceleration" in shopping ahead of the peak holiday season.
"We're monitoring the trends, and we're going to remain agile as we respond to the changing business trends," Dickson said.
Here's how the company performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
For the quarter, Gap reported net income of $311 million, or 86 cents per share, compared with $236 million, or 62 cents per share, the year prior. Sales rose slightly from $3.94 billion the year prior.
At Athleta, net sales were down 14% compared with last year, coming in at $220 million. Comparable sales for the banner sank 15%, which the company attributed to "limited traction" from efforts to modernize its merchandise and marketing.
The company's namesake brand saw 9% comparable sales growth for the quarter, with net sales of $1.1 billion, marking an 11% increase compared with last year. Dickson said it was the brand's 12th consecutive quarter of positive comparable sales.
"Gap is really firing on all cylinders, and the consistency of the brand is really giving us confidence in the brand's ability to continue its momentum," Dickson said.
The Old Navy banner saw flat comparable sales for the quarter and net sales of $2.3 billion, up 1% compared with last year. It's the first earnings report since the brand, which has been experiencing sluggish sales, named Michael Francis as its new CEO last quarter. Francis began his role at Old Navy on Nov. 2.
Banana Republic saw its net sales sink 3% compared with last year, which the company attributed to delayed demand for cold-weather categories and a women's fall assortment that fell flat. Wall Street had been expecting growth of 1.5%, according to StreetAccount.
Dickson said the brand has since introduced new products and seen demand "rebound" as cooler weather has set in across the country.
"We've been encouraged by the early customer response, and we should see sequential improvement in the fourth quarter," he said. "There's some work to do here, but with peak selling still ahead, I'm confident that the team is focused on the right areas and [will] ultimately position Banana well for growth."

articles.title_orig: Is Nvidia Stock a Once-in-a-Decade Buying Opportunity After Its Latest Earnings?
articles.title_zh: Is Nvidia Stock a Once-in-a-Decade Buying Opportunity After Its Latest Earnings?
articles.content_orig:
By Prosper Junior Bakiny – Nov 19, 2026 at 4:15PM EST
10 stocks we like better than Nvidia ›
The past week has been hard on Nvidia ( NVDA -3.30% ) . The semiconductor leader had to separate from its co-founder and now-former CEO, Jensen Huang, after he was embroiled in a scandal involving alleged extramarital affairs, including with a woman believed to be a Chinese intelligence asset. Colette Kress, who remains CFO, has stepped up as interim CEO, leading the company through its first quarterly update since Huang's departure.
And what an update it was. Nvidia once again crushed expectations, but that wasn't enough to jolt the stock, which remains down significantly since it reached a new all-time high in early October. Is Nvidia a generational buying opportunity at current levels?
Death, taxes, and Nvidia's financial results coming in above analysts' projections seem to be the only certain things these days. In the third quarter of its fiscal year 2027, which ended on Oct. 25, the company's revenue came in at $115.8 billion, up 103% compared to the year-ago period. Data center revenue grew 110% year over year to $107.6 billion.
Nvidia's non-GAAP gross margin was 74.9%, compared to the 73.5% reported in the prior-year quarter. The semiconductor specialist's non-GAAP operating income was $77.9 billion, rising 116% year over year, while its non-GAAP earnings per share were $2.68, up 111% year over year.
The fact that profits are growing faster than revenue is a strong sign for Nvidia, given the industry's increasing competitiveness. While some investors worry that competition from custom AI chips will erode the company's pricing power in the GPU ( graphics processing unit ) market, as hyperscalers and other corporations increasingly opt for these custom chips, it seems, at least, that this hasn't happened yet. Improving margins are a sign that Nvidia maintains strong pricing power.
Meanwhile, Nvidia's free cash flow for the period was $43.8 billion, rising 98% year over year. The company also posted excellent guidance. Nvidia expects $130 billion in revenue (at the midpoint) for its fourth quarter. That would represent a 91% year-over-year increase.
NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/19/26
Of course, Nvidia's financial results and guidance were only part of the story. The market wants to know how the company's efforts to replace Huang are going. Nvidia said it isn't interested in bringing back Huang, despite many people, both inside and outside the company, calling for his reinstatement. And it is actively looking for a replacement, although nobody knows when Nvidia will find someone to step into the CEO role permanently. In my opinion, that's both good and bad.
It's bad because the longer this search drags on, the more uncertainty it could add to the company's prospects. But it's good because replacing a CEO as effective as Huang isn't an easy task, and the company's board is rightfully taking the time it needs to do so, or so it seems. In the meantime, several factors highlight just how massive an opportunity Nvidia could still tap into, even as it faces a more stringent regulatory environment.
During the recent U.S. midterm elections, voters elected many lawmakers and politicians across various states who had promised to be stricter on the AI industry . This may result in delayed permits and slower data center build-outs. However, Nvidia expects a great year ahead. The company raised its guidance for the fiscal year 2028, which covers most of the calendar year 2027.
The company now expects revenue to grow 75% in fiscal year 2028, up from its previous projection of 70% -- and that's after also raising its guidance for its current fiscal year. If we assume Nvidia's fourth-quarter revenue lands at the midpoint, it could generate $423.7 billion this fiscal year and $741.4 billion next year, based on its projected 75% growth rate.
So, given its current market cap of $3.8 trillion, Nvidia is trading at 5.1x estimated fiscal year 2028 revenue -- that's more than fair for a company growing as fast as it is, in my view. However, the CEO search does introduce some uncertainty. And we still have to account for the risk of margin erosion as industry competition intensifies. So, what's the verdict?
Nvidia looks like a buy at current levels, but it's hardly a once-in-a-decade buying opportunity. Still, investors who purchase the company's shares today could see strong returns over the medium term.

articles.title_orig: AMD Slides After Hunterbrook Shorts Stock, Cites Circular Deals
articles.title_zh: AMD Slides After Hunterbrook Shorts Stock, Cites Circular Deals
articles.content_orig:
Shares of chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices close down 7.72% to $489.19 Thursday after investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report alleging that the company "has its own China problem."
Hunterbrook disclosed that it had taken a short position in AMD.
The report claims that "after the U.S. blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT Systems, the company kept getting newer AMD firmware, which enables AMD chips to run in servers."
CNBC did not independently verify this information.
Hunterbrook also said that new export rules in Washington could "tighten restrictions on AMD's foreign business," alleging that AMD "bills over 20% of its revenue to customers in China and Hong Kong," and "depends on a Chinese partner to finish most of its chips."
The allegations come amid investigations of rival chipmaker Nvidia over its sales to companies in Asia with ties to China. AMD has been viewed as a beneficiary of the uncertainty surrounding Nvidia.
"The claims misrepresent AMD's business practices and relationships," an AMD spokesperson said in a statement. "AMD complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations. We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity."
Lisa Su, CEO of AMD, told investors on the company's recent earnings call that China is an "important" market and that the semiconductor giant wants to be fully compliant with U.S. export controls.
AMD continued to slide after-hours, trading down 0.45% to $487 shortly after 4 p.m.

articles.title_orig: Next year’s iPhone Pro redesign sounds like exactly what I’ve been wanting
articles.title_zh: Next year’s iPhone Pro redesign sounds like exactly what I’ve been wanting
articles.content_orig:
Next year's "iPhone 20 Pro" models will use the same glass design as the iPhone Air , but with more pronounced curvature along all four sides, according to the leaker known as " Fixed Focus Digital ."
In a new post on Weibo, the leaker said the device would use the same glass material as the ‌iPhone Air‌, adjusted to have greater curvature and produce a four-sided curved effect. The accompanying hashtag refers specifically to an "iPhone 20 Pro" with a four-sided curved, "all-glass" design.
An illustration shared with the post depicts rounded front and rear glass meeting a narrow, polished, gold-colored metallic frame. Physical side buttons, antenna lines, and a protruding rear camera assembly remain visible.
Taken together with earlier rumors and the post's accompanying illustration, the repeated comparisons suggest a design somewhere between the iPhone X and ‌iPhone Air‌. The ‌iPhone Air‌ provides a reference for the slim profile and a more modern iPhone design, while the more pronounced glass curvature recalls the rounded edges of the iPhone X. Both feature a polished frame.
The latest claim builds on Fixed Focus Digital's previous report that Apple had modified ‌iPhone Air‌ manufacturing equipment to produce more rounded glass components for the 20th anniversary models. The leaker said the changes had helped reduce manufacturing costs, while substantially improving thinness and heat dissipation.
In a still-earlier report , the same leaker also claimed that a supply chain facility had completed renovations ahead of "iPhone 20" production, with manufacturing quality expected to be roughly comparable to the first-generation ‌iPhone Air‌. The ‌iPhone Air‌ features Ceramic Shield 2 on the front and Ceramic Shield on the back.
The broader design picture aligns with Bloomberg 's Mark Gurman 's reporting that Apple's anniversary Pro models will feature glass that curves into the sides from both the front and rear, with a thin metal band between the two panels. Gurman has also described thinner display bezels and curved glass around all corners and edges, in what he expects to be the biggest overhaul of the Pro line since the iPhone X.
Apple's 20th-anniversary iPhone models are expected to launch in the fall of 2027 . While leakers have variably referred to the device as the "iPhone 20 Pro," Apple's naming plans remain unclear. It seems plausible that the company could skip the iPhone 19 name to emphasize the anniversary, similar to its introduction of the iPhone X in 2017.

articles.title_orig: Trump, Xi and Putin meet as global alliances hang in the balance
articles.title_zh: Trump, Xi and Putin meet as global alliances hang in the balance
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
SHENZHEN, China — Donald Trump met Thursday with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at a villa in southern China, an unprecedented gathering of a U.S. president with Washington’s chief geopolitical rivals bent on undermining American power.
The meeting, conceived not by policymakers but by Trump and Putin themselves, had a fractured agenda, with each leader coming to the table with divergent interests and different stakes .
But the image of Trump standing alongside Putin and Xi — then sitting alone with the two of them, at a great round table in a cacophonous hall — was itself the culmination of a decade of his foreign policy thinking , a great-man theory of diplomacy that has broken with American tradition, elevating authoritarian leaders over democratic allies.
The U.S. president appeared subdued, thanking Xi and Putin before turning to the press.
“No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement and speech,” he said, arguing he had a “special responsibility” to maintain dialogue with adversarial world powers. “We are really making history.”
Unlike at Yalta, in 1945, when President Franklin D. Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet Premier Josef Stalin famously gathered to shape the postwar order, the American leader was not at the center of these photographs. That place of honor belonged to Xi, the host, who presided over the gathering at a remote retreat outside the city.
It was a portrait of a nation asserting its place among the world’s superpowers — the very image Beijing had sought in agreeing to host the extraordinary gathering.
“History tells us that when great powers are at peace, the world is secure,” Xi said. “When great powers clash, the world is in chaos.”
The competing agendas could make the summit little more than a spectacle, yet still produce images that harken back to the famous Yalta conference of 1945.
It was not immediately clear when the meeting concluded, after roughly an hour and a half, whether the three leaders had reached any substantive understandings. They were expected to discuss arms control and the wars in Iran and Ukraine, among other matters.
An initial readout of the meeting first released by the Russian side listed four points of agreement, broadly committing to work to uphold international security, minimize nuclear risks, increase petroleum output and, most specifically,  overhaul the United Nations and the International Criminal Court, which it said “must not abuse their jurisdiction.”
The court has a warrant outstanding for Putin’s arrest.
Putin framed the trilateral meeting as one of equals, elevating a Russian Federation that has been economically and militarily devastated, and ostracized from the international community, over its war against Ukraine. Russian state media highlighted Xi’s decision to place Putin to his right throughout the summit as a gesture of honor.
“I am convinced that Russia, China and the United States, our peoples, are capable of making a significant contribution to strengthening security and stability in the world,” Putin said, “if they cooperate constructively as partners on the basis of mutual respect, equality and a balance of interests.”
The Russian leader appeared almost giddy throughout the day’s meetings, and upon departing Shenzhen for the airport, escorted personally by Xi to his car, was heard saying, “I don’t think anyone ever expected everything to go so well.”
“The trilateral summit was a giant gift to Putin. It put him on a stage where he does not belong,” Michael McFaul, a former U.S. ambassador to Russia now at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, told The Times. “The photo of that meeting will be seen throughout the world, making it look like Putin is a respected leader of a great power. What did Americans get in return? Nothing, absolutely nothing.”
The unusual summit comes just weeks after Trump suffered a generational rebuke in the midterm elections and as he remains bogged down in a war with Iran, which threatened to erupt in a new round of hostilities in the coming days.
Publicly, Trump framed the gathering as an effort to curb nuclear proliferation. Yet instead of advancing a trilateral nonproliferation agreement among the world’s three largest nuclear powers, Putin offered a message of defiance, sending nuclear-capable bombers to nearby Vietnam a day before the summit in a rare deployment. China, meanwhile, rebuffed calls to slow down its breakneck nuclear buildup currently dwarfed by America’s arsenal.
The Trump administration let the last remaining U.S. arms control agreement with Russia expire earlier this year.
“Despite the talk of denuclearization by the Trump administration, no staff members prepped the president to meaningfully discuss this topic with Putin or Xi, who are unwilling partners for restraints and guardrails,” said Jennifer Hong, senior director of the Institute for Indo-Pacific Security.
Instead, Trump’s focus seems to have turned to ensuring nonproliferation not among world powers, but in the Middle East — the main justification he has given for launching war against Tehran earlier this year.
“We’re not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon,” he said at the top of the meeting.
Putin had hoped the summit would secure space and time to continue executing his war against Ukraine — a prospect that Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelensky, took seriously as the meeting was about to begin.
“Big countries always think that they can make decisions about the future of all the world,” Zelensky told NBC News. “It’s a huge mistake.”
Sitting alongside Xi, Trump said the two of them were looking to “help with respect to the war with Russia and Ukraine” and “would like to see it ended.”
Few independent analysts believe Putin is interested in ending the war in its current state. But at the trilateral engagement, Trump suggested Zelensky was responsible for Moscow’s continued attempts at conquest. “Things are happening,” Trump said. “I think that he, and I hope the other side, would like to see an end to that war.”
The meetings were Trump’s first with Putin since the two held a summit last year in Alaska, a gathering that failed to produce a breakthrough in Trump’s attempts to bring an end to the deadliest conflict in Europe since World War II.
Trump met individually with both Putin and Xi ahead of the trilateral gathering, despite White House officials insisting before the trip that a direct meeting with Putin was not on the agenda.
“Who is he? He’s my friend,” Trump said, walking toward Putin with an outstretched hand.
“We have had a great relationship for many years. We’ve known each other for a long time,” Trump added. “And I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start.”
A Russian diplomat attending the conference with Putin told reporters that Trump and Putin together are “committed to a peaceful resolution to the Ukrainian conflict, though the Europeans are clearly trying to stand in the way.”
European officials have been wary of the Shenzhen summit, warning against the future of Ukraine being negotiated without Ukrainians present. A Chinese official told The Times they would have been welcome to attend, but no invitation was formally extended.
Xi greeted Trump at the steps of Air Force One upon his arrival in Shenzhen on Wednesday evening, reciprocating the rare honor Trump extended to the Chinese leader at Joint Base Andrews outside Washington in September.
While Trump’s meetings with Xi were the primary purpose of his visit, the Chinese leader is also hosting a major international conference, gathering leaders from around the world for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, known as APEC.

articles.title_orig: Live updates: Russia shifts on Ukraine NATO pledges after Trump-Putin-Xi talks
articles.title_zh: Live updates: Russia shifts on Ukraine NATO pledges after Trump-Putin-Xi talks
articles.content_orig:
European leaders have said they are ready for negotiations with Russia on ending the war in Ukraine, in a strong show of support for Kyiv.
"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".
They were speaking at Berlin's summit of Ukraine's allies known as the Coalition of the Willing.
Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side". Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks.
Trump had earlier held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen , south-eastern China, with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping and later dialled into the Berlin summit from Air Force One.
In a lengthy press conference following his talks with Trump and Xi, Putin addressed the question of multilateral peace talks, saying the Americans were "insistently" asking Russia to allow the Europeans to take part.
Putin claimed Russia was not against the idea but said Moscow wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".
"That is why, through diplomatic channels, we have invited the Europeans to come to Moscow in order to determine their positions. And after that, we will decide in what format we will continue the dialogue with Ukraine."
But Putin also said that "every day" Russia heard that European leaders were talking about war coming in 2030. "But we are not planning to attack anyone... Is that normal? I do not think so," he said. Still, Putin added, Russia understood that "discussing issues linked to security in Europe is pointless without the Europeans".
Jared Kushner told reporters that the US president had come away from Shenzhen believing that "peace is achievable".
Striking an upbeat note, Kushner said that the Russians were willing to trust the instinct of the US envoys "on our behalf" that the Europeans should be at the table and that Moscow was now "comfortable" with Ukraine having security guarantees based on the idea enshrined in Nato's Article Five that requires allies to come to a country's defence if it comes under attack.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who also was at the summit in Germany's capital, has long sought a guarantee equivalent to Nato's collective defence clause, and there has been little indication that Putin would accept that kind of condition.
Russia rejects outright the idea of Ukrainian membership of Nato, but reports say US negotiators have mulled the idea of giving Kyiv Article Five-style guarantees without being part of the Western defensive alliance if it agrees to painful territorial concessions.
Zelensky and the three European leaders – Merz, Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron – were not as upbeat as Kushner, and the Ukrainian president made clear that the Russian president had spurned every proposal so far: "Putin has always said no."
The German chancellor was equally sceptical, although he said with US involvement the chance of peace was increasing. Europe was willing to enter "serious discussions on European security" with Russia, he explained, "as long as it's matched with a serious discussion and only first a peace agreement with Ukraine".
"These talks have to begin, and we will accept if conditions are acceptable for Europe and Ukraine," said Merz.
He also said any attempts to divide Europe into spheres of influence run by major powers was unacceptable, amid concerns on the continent that this issue may have been on the agenda at the trilateral talks in Shenzhen.
"A 'Yalta format' will not bring peace," Merz said, referring to the post-World War Two agreement between the US, the USSR and Britain in 1945.
Meanwhile, Macron urged Ukraine's allies to do the "maximum" to deliver the much-needed air defence systems Kyiv needed to repel deadly Russian attacks.
The French leader also urged the allies to "reopen the question" of Ukraine's membership in Nato.
There have been mixed messages from Moscow on European participation to the talks. Last week, following a visit to Moscow, the US envoys, Steve Witkoff and Kushner, appeared certain that Europe would soon have a seat at the negotiating table.
But the Russians were more circumspect and this week Putin's aide Yury Ushakov said a "great deal" would have to be done before the format could be expanded, suggesting that several more rounds of discussions would have to be held before any four-sided talks could take place.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
While Russia has engaged with several rounds of talks over the last year, little in Moscow's rhetoric or actions suggests that the Kremlin is considering scaling down its war on Ukraine.
It continues to pound Kyiv's energy infrastructure to cripple it as winter takes hold, increasing numbers of civilian casualties are being recorded across the country, and Kremlin officials have not budged from Russia's demands for Ukrainian sovereign territory.
As delegations were meeting in China and Germany on Thursday, several buildings in Kyiv's historic centre came under attack from drones. One person was killed in a strike on a residential building in the Podilskyi neighbourhood, while the Dutch and Austrian embassies as well as Saint Volodymyr's Cathedral reported damage.
And Putin also vowed that Moscow's response to a Ukrainian strike on the Crimean Bridge linking Russia with occupied Crimea would be "considerably more painful" than what Kyiv had achieved.
He also said he had discussed a "possible ceasefire in a number of areas" but had decided against it after the attack on the bridge.
Still, Putin claimed to be "interested" in ending the war and was ready to make compromises, while Ukraine and Europe were not.
"I assure you, we have no desire at all to continue this armed conflict," Putin said, despite the fact that Russia has in recent months intensified its attacks on Ukraine's critical infrastructure as cold winter approaches.
Kyiv and its European allies say that – in the absence of any major success on the vast front line – the Kremlin leader is seeking to break Ukrainian resistance by leaving millions of civilians without electricity and water supply.

articles.title_orig: Trump accused of falling asleep during Xi Jinping speech at Apec summit in China
articles.title_zh: Trump accused of falling asleep during Xi Jinping speech at Apec summit in China
articles.content_orig:
US president appeared to doze off while Chinese leader made speech, but White House insisted he was awake
Donald Trump was, again, accused of falling asleep during a televised event, this time during the speech of the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in China.
The US president appeared to close his eyes for roughly 10 seconds on Thursday. As his eyes closed, Trump’s head tilted downward, and his hands remained clasped in front of him.
Several prominent Trump critics on social media alleged that the US president was asleep, including Republicans Against Trump , California governor Gavin Newsom’s press office and conservative lawyer George Conway .
White House officials denied the allegations, claiming the 80-year-old US president was looking down at papers in front of him.
“Fake News! President Trump was looking at papers in front of him while the speaker made remarks. You can clearly see his eyes move back and forth,” Steven Cheung, the White House director of communications, wrote on X in response to a Newsweek article.
“This is why the people despise media so much. They constantly lie,” Cheung added.
Trump often faces accusations of falling asleep during televised events such as Oval Office press conferences, cabinet meetings and sporting events.
Occasionally, while listening to other people speak, the US president will close his eyes for several seconds, appearing as though he is falling asleep . Despite footage of the instances going viral, the White House and Trump allies have insisted the US president does not fall asleep during meetings.
Administration officials have excused Trump’s apparent drowsiness as blinking or an example of the president listening intently. They consistently claim Trump “doesn’t sleep”.
Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, testified to lawmakers earlier this year that he had “never seen” Trump fall asleep.
“On the contrary, the guy doesn’t sleep, which is a big problem because he calls me at two in the morning,” Rubio said in June.
Last year, JD Vance said that Trump hardly ever sleeps, even while traveling overnight.
“If we go on a 20-hour trip somewhere, he doesn’t sleep the entire time. And of course, if he’s not sleeping, if he’s working, he expects everybody else to be working too,” Vance told Fox News .
Trump became the oldest US president ever inaugurated when he was sworn in nearly two years ago. Despite his age, Trump often claims he is in near-perfect health , often bragging about his “perfect” cognitive test results and insisting he has a lot of energy.

articles.title_orig: AMD Stock Drops After Short Report Says It Isn’t an Nvidia Replacement
articles.title_zh: AMD Stock Drops After Short Report Says It Isn’t an Nvidia Replacement
articles.content_orig:
Shares of chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices close down 7.72% to $489.19 on Thursday after investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report alleging that the company "has its own China problem."
Hunterbrook disclosed that it had taken a short position in AMD.
The report claims that "after the U.S. blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT Systems, the company kept getting newer AMD firmware, which enables AMD chips to run in servers."
CNBC did not independently verify this information.
Hunterbrook also said that new export rules in Washington could "tighten restrictions on AMD's foreign business," alleging that AMD "bills over 20% of its revenue to customers in China and Hong Kong," and "depends on a Chinese partner to finish most of its chips."
The allegations come amid investigations of rival chipmaker Nvidia over its sales to companies in Asia with ties to China. AMD has been viewed as a beneficiary of the uncertainty surrounding Nvidia.
"The claims misrepresent AMD's business practices and relationships," an AMD spokesperson said in a statement. "AMD complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations. We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity."
Lisa Su, CEO of AMD, told investors on the company's recent earnings call that China is an "important" market and that the semiconductor giant wants to be fully compliant with U.S. export controls.
AMD continued to slide after hours, trading down 0.45% to $487 shortly after 4 p.m.

articles.title_orig: Commerce approved sales of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies, Rep. Mast says
articles.title_zh: Commerce approved sales of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies, Rep. Mast says
articles.content_orig:
The subagency of the Commerce Department that regulates and enforces exports approved the sale of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies including Alibaba and Tencent as of May 2026, according to documents released Thursday by the House Foreign Affairs Committee.
Some of those approvals, made by Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, included sales to companies designated by the Department of Defense as "Chinese Military Companies," according to the documents. From December through May, there had been 3.4 million requested sales of U.S. AI chips to China, the committee reported, citing those made by Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices .
"Over the past month, the administration's handling of chip export controls has put our national security and technology edge at risk. The Bureau of Industry and Security has failed to enforce the rules, and Congress must now conduct rigorous oversight of the administration's policies," Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said at a meeting of the panel Thursday at which members voted to release the documents.
Spokespersons for Nvidia and AMD said their companies comply with U.S. export control laws.
Nvidia argued it was following the Commerce Department regulations that were in effect at the time.
"The review and licensing process spanned more than half a year, with approvals subject to strict conditions and limited volumes. Despite receiving some licenses, we have since stopped shipping H200s to China," Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo told CNBC.
On Tuesday, Nvidia reported $2.4 billion in quarterly revenue from H200 and related chip sales in China. In total, customers based in China and Hong Kong made up about 9.5% of all revenue.
"AMD complies with applicable U.S. export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations," AMD said through a spokesperson.
The approval of 879,000 AI chip is "not that many," Bernstein Senior Analyst Stacy Rasgon told CNBC, adding that this news is not surprising.
"It doesn't sound to me like they're approving everything they got willy nilly," Rasgon said of the Commerce Department. With 879,000 approvals out of 3.4 million requested AI chip sales, he added, "There was a process in place, and it sounds like they approved about one out of every four."
Despite a rapid succession of China export controls on AI chips that started under the Biden administration in 2022, Nvidia and AMD both re-engineered some chips to comply and be sold legally in China. And in December, Trump said Nvidia could ship H200s, its older generation Hopper chips, to "approved customers in China" if the U.S. got a 25% cut of sales.
The U.S. then licensed Nvidia H200 sales to Alibaba , Tencent, ByteDance and other Chinese companies, although sales were limited because Beijing didn't approve large-scale imports, chip analyst Patrick Moorhead of Moor Insights & Strategy told CNBC last week.
H200 sales numbers remained low due to those restrictions on China's end. Nvidia said H200 shipments to China made up less than 1% of data center revenue for the quarter that ended in July.
"In the grand context of the size of this market and how much they're shipping, it's a rounding error. It's tiny," Rasgon told CNBC.
The committee cited the Export Control Reform Act as justification for releasing the data. The panel said the law allows it to declassify and release export data if it "determines that the withholding of the following information is contrary to the national interest."
The Commerce Department did not respond to a request for comment. The license requests released by the Foreign Affairs Committee include requests to sell to major firms including Bytedance, Tesla (Shanghai) and Baidu .
The release of documents comes in the wake of Jensen Huang 's resignation from the chip supplier Nvidia after news surfaced that he had several extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy that led to concerns about Nvidia chips being diverted to China.
In the weeks since, Republicans and Democrats in Congress have called for legislation to be passed that would impose stricter export controls on the sale of advanced AI chips to China and other adversaries.
"The license information we are disclosing today will help inform the American public about how BIS has handled licenses for Nvidia H200 and equivalent AMD chips to China. The public has the right to know how these decisions were made," Meeks said.
Mast said two of the firms listed in Nvidia license applications to BIS —  Maginfra and New Matrix — are suspected "smuggling fronts." The New York Times reported in November that both companies had empty offices and had ties to companies under national security sanctions.
"Both are fake companies. If BIS approved the sale of these chips to these firms, obviously that is of tremendous concern to us — especially given that President Trump made clear last year that the sale of any AI chips to China will have very real national security conditions," Mast said at the Thursday meeting.
Maginfra and New Matrix did not reply to requests for comment.
Shares of AMD fell Thursday after the investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report alleging the company "has its own China problem." The report claims that "after the U.S. blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT Systems, the company kept getting newer AMD firmware, which enables AMD chips to run in servers."
CNBC did not independently verify this information.
Fallout from the Huang scandal on Capitol Hill has intensified in the last week, as lawmakers question the degree to which the former head of Nvidia's relationship with the suspected Chinese spy could have jeopardized national security and American AI dominance.
Huang is due for a closed-door transcribed interview with the House Foreign Affairs panel and two other committees on Dec. 1. Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter is scheduled to appear before the panels Dec. 2.
Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., announced on CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had also agreed to testify.
Lutnick has come under fire over his relationship to Huang and for his failure to take action on Megaspeed , the Singaporean company where Alice Huang , with whom the former Nvidia CEO had an affair, was an executive until 2025. U.S. investigators suspect Megaspeed diverted Nvidia chips to China.
Amid that criticism, the Commerce Department on Monday issued an interim final rule to close a loophole that has allowed Chinese companies lease Nvidia's advancing computing power from data centers in third controls.
The rule was "written by and at the direction of" the Treasury Department and the White House National Security Council, BIS said in a press release.
— Megan Cassella , Daren Fonda and Kif Leswing contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Trump touts ‘unbelievable’ summit with Putin and Xi, though peace deals remain elusive
articles.title_zh: Trump touts ‘unbelievable’ summit with Putin and Xi, though peace deals remain elusive
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
SHENZHEN, China — Donald Trump met Thursday with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at a villa in southern China, an unprecedented gathering of a U.S. president with Washington’s chief geopolitical rivals bent on undermining American power.
The meeting, conceived not by policymakers but by Trump and Putin, had a fractured agenda, with each leader coming to the table with divergent interests and different stakes.
As they dispersed to their capitals, the presidents had few tangible gains to show for a summit hastily assembled in a matter of weeks, bypassing the months of groundwork that typically underpin diplomatic breakthroughs.
But the image of Trump standing alongside Putin and Xi — then sitting alone with the two of them, at a great round table in a cacophonous hall — was itself the culmination of a decade of his foreign policy thinking, a great-man theory of diplomacy that has broken with American tradition, elevating authoritarian leaders over democratic allies.
The U.S. president appeared subdued, thanking Xi and Putin before turning to journalists.
“No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement and speech,” he said, arguing he had a “special responsibility” to maintain dialogue with adversarial world powers. “We are really making history.”
Unlike at Yalta in 1945, when President Franklin D. Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet Premier Josef Stalin famously gathered to shape the postwar order, the American leader was not at the center of these photographs. That place of honor belonged to Xi, the host, who presided over the gathering at a remote retreat outside the city.
It was a portrait of a nation asserting its place among the world’s superpowers — the very image Beijing had sought in agreeing to host the extraordinary gathering.
“History tells us that when great powers are at peace, the world is secure,” Xi said. “When great powers clash, the world is in chaos.”
The competing agendas could make the summit little more than a spectacle, yet still produce images that harken back to the famous Yalta conference of 1945.
But if any substantive understandings were reached behind closed doors, none of them were released to the public.
The summit’s pageantry fit a familiar pattern for Trump, who has repeatedly staged headline-grabbing encounters with controversial leaders only to walk away empty-handed. Three high-stakes meetings with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during his first term failed to meaningfully shift relations between Washington and Pyongyang, and a meeting with Putin in Anchorage last year likewise failed to generate progress toward ending Russia’s war in Ukraine.
This time, the spectacular gathering lasted just an hour and a half, and produced only a readout of four points of agreement, broadly committing to work to uphold international security, minimize nuclear risks, increase petroleum output and, most specifically, overhaul the United Nations and the International Criminal Court, which it said “must not abuse their jurisdiction.”
The court has a warrant outstanding for Putin’s arrest.
Putin framed the trilateral meeting as one of equals, elevating a Russian Federation that has been economically and militarily devastated, and ostracized from the international community, over its war against Ukraine. Russian state media highlighted Xi’s decision to place Putin to his right throughout the summit as a gesture of honor.
“I am convinced that Russia, China and the United States, our peoples, are capable of making a significant contribution to strengthening security and stability in the world,” Putin said, “if they cooperate constructively as partners on the basis of mutual respect, equality and a balance of interests.”
The Russian leader appeared almost giddy throughout the day’s meetings, and upon departing Shenzhen for the airport, escorted personally by Xi to his car, was heard saying, “I don’t think anyone ever expected everything to go so well.”
“The trilateral summit was a giant gift to Putin. It put him on a stage where he does not belong,” Michael McFaul, a former U.S. ambassador to Russia now at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, told The Times. “The photo of that meeting will be seen throughout the world, making it look like Putin is a respected leader of a great power. What did Americans get in return? Nothing, absolutely nothing.”
The unusual summit comes just weeks after Trump suffered a generational rebuke in the midterm elections and as he remains bogged down in a war with Iran, which threatened to erupt in a new round of hostilities in the coming days.
Publicly, Trump framed the gathering as an effort to curb nuclear proliferation. Yet instead of advancing a trilateral nonproliferation agreement among the world’s three largest nuclear powers, Putin offered a message of defiance, sending nuclear-capable bombers to nearby Vietnam a day before the summit in a rare deployment. China, meanwhile, rebuffed calls to slow down its breakneck nuclear buildup currently dwarfed by America’s arsenal.
The Trump administration let the last remaining U.S. arms control agreement with Russia expire earlier this year.
“Despite the talk of denuclearization by the Trump administration, no staff members prepped the president to meaningfully discuss this topic with Putin or Xi, who are unwilling partners for restraints and guardrails,” said Jennifer Hong, senior director of the Institute for Indo-Pacific Security.
Instead, Trump’s focus seems to have turned to ensuring nonproliferation not among world powers, but in the Middle East — the main justification he has given for launching war against the Islamic Republic this year.
“We’re not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon,” he said at the start of the meeting.
Putin had hoped the summit would secure space and time to continue executing his war against Ukraine — a prospect that Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelensky, took seriously as the meeting was about to begin.
“Big countries always think that they can make decisions about the future of all the world,” Zelensky told NBC News. “It’s a huge mistake.”
Sitting alongside Xi, Trump said the two of them were looking to “help with respect to the war with Russia and Ukraine” and “would like to see it ended.”
Few independent analysts believe Putin is interested in ending the war in its current state. But at the trilateral engagement, Trump suggested Zelensky was responsible for Moscow’s continued attempts at conquest. “Things are happening,” Trump said. “I think that [Putin] and I hope the other side, would like to see an end to that war.”
The meetings were Trump’s first with Putin since their summit last year in Alaska, a gathering that failed to produce a breakthrough in the Republican president’s attempts to bring an end to the deadliest conflict in Europe since World War II.
Trump met individually with  Putin and Xi ahead of the trilateral gathering despite White House officials insisting before the trip that a direct meeting with Putin was not on the agenda.
“Who is he? He’s my friend,” Trump said, walking toward Putin with an outstretched hand.
“We have had a great relationship for many years. We’ve known each other for a long time,” Trump added. “And I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start.”
A Russian diplomat attending the conference with Putin told reporters that Trump and Putin together are “committed to a peaceful resolution to the Ukrainian conflict, though the Europeans are clearly trying to stand in the way.”
European officials have been wary of the Shenzhen summit, warning against the future of Ukraine being negotiated without Ukrainians present. A Chinese official told The Times they would have been welcome to attend, but no invitation was formally extended.

articles.title_orig: There’s Comfort In Conquering The Past
articles.title_zh: There’s Comfort In Conquering The Past
articles.content_orig:
2:34 PM EST on November 19, 2026
The first time I played The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time was during a hurricane. It was late 1999, I was 10 years old, Hurricane Irene was bearing down on Miami, and my friend Ryan had come over to spend the night. He had brought his copy of Ocarina of Time , the game a year old at that point, and his plan was that we should play it all the way to the end. This was a bold goal for two idiot preteen boys, and though we plowed through the entire Child Link part of the game and the start of Adult Link's quest to release the temple sages, the Water Temple claimed us as its own. We didn't have a Prima strategy guide or the internet to help us out, so after hours (and I do mean hours) of raising and lowering water levels, we gave up. I didn't end up beating my own copy of Ocarina of Time , which my dad bought for me as soon as the hurricane passed, until the next summer in Venezuela, but even then, even as an idiot preteen boy, I knew I had played something special.
Twenty-seven years later, I am playing something special again. Well, I am playing the same thing again, but newer, fresher, and more beautiful. I am playing the remake of Ocarina of Time , and I have loved every second of it so far. As a remake, this is a work of art. The graphics are gorgeous, if a bit shiny. The story is as good as it ever was, only now with a lot more voice acting that gives characters personality. The gameplay is much the same, albeit with some quality-of-life changes; the ability to swap equipped items with one button is a huge upgrade to pausing and going into the menu every three seconds. I'm not saying that the remake is now the best way to play Ocarina of Time —there's something to be said for the friction that came with the original's technical limitations—but I am saying that the remake justifies its own existence with an attention to detail and a commitment to thrilling gameplay that shines through in every second of playtime.
In my time with the remake, I have learned to love the quirks and anxieties of a game that is rightfully considered among the very best to ever exist. I have also remembered that when Ocarina of Time gets something right, there's nothing like it. The puzzles are never too confusing, but they have a tactile pacing that makes every step towards the solution feel like a victory. The way the game teaches you to play it is unrivaled. It all fits like a perfect jigsaw, never throwing too much at the player while still challenging them to think creatively. I'm not one for adventure games in this vein anymore, which is probably why I have only played a few Zelda games since Ocarina and its sequel, but every time I opened a previously locked door, I had the forbidden thought of, "Should I play the whole Zelda series now?" There's no higher praise from me than saying Ocarina has me wondering if I should play Skyward Sword .
Ocarina of Time isn't the only blast from the past I've played recently. I have played World of Warcraft off and mostly on since early 2005, and I have tried every variation that the game has had to offer over that time. There is what people call "retail," which is the default game that has progressed from its messy origins to now, 11 expansions later. Retail these days feels like a completely different game than what I started playing, which isn't necessarily a bad thing. In 2019, Blizzard, the game's developers, caved to massive player pressure and released World of Warcraft Classic , essentially launching the game again from scratch, but with some changes to make it a bit more modern.
Classic was a big success, and has continued on since then. As the years of Classic went on, however, players wanted more. They wanted what was deemed " Classic Plus ," essentially the old game but with more twists and turns and new gameplay additions. Blizzard listened with Season of Discovery in 2023. This mode added a lot of abilities from later WoW as well as some new roles for long-time classes. For example, mages could now be healers and shamans could be grossly overpowered tanks. SoD was an even bigger success than Classic , all things considered, because it showed that the skeleton of WoW could support a new evolution.
That brings us to World of Warcraft: Forever , the new game mode that launched on Nov. 4 to record-breaking numbers. It seems that anyone and everyone who had ever played some form of WoW dipped into Forever to check it out. What is it, though? Forever is what Blizzard intends to be a different evolution of Classic . Classes got new tools and toys to play with, but they are not as wild as in SoD . Instead, Blizzard made everyone a bit stronger, a bit more fun to play, but still very much in the realm of old-school gameplay. The innovations instead seem to be coming from the new things players can do. Forever has added new zones in the open world, new dungeons to explore, and starting next month, new raids for groups of 10, 20, or 40 people.
In other words, Forever is an alternate timeline in which Blizzard decided to never release expansion packs, and instead keep everyone's max level at 60 and progress them horizontally. This allows the developers the ability to explore parts of the original world that were under-served, and turn them into new adventures with that Classic vibe. Forever is a much cozier game than what Retail WoW has become, much slower in its gameplay and progression. As the name implies, there is no rush here; this is meant to last as long as players keep logging in, and that makes everything feel more meaningful. The new weapon you got, or the new piece of armor, or a fancy trinket that gives you special powers ... all of those things are meant to, in some way or another, last for the duration of your character's lifespan, rather than getting replaced every four months with a new season.
I have not quit Retail WoW , but I fully took a break to dive into Forever when it released. In the two weeks since, I have played an obscene amount— Forever added viable controller support, so I've been playing on my laptop on the couch while watching TV—and have gotten my first character, a shaman, to level 60. It took me four days, 20 hours, and 29 minutes played to do so. Forever has taken over. Add in the roughly 12 hours of Ocarina of Time that have gotten me to the precipice of the Water Temple, and I've been living in video game past almost exclusively this month.
Though I've enjoyed wrapping myself in the warmth of nostalgia, what I've found most satisfying about this extended foray into the past is the usefulness of my familiarity. I'd consider myself an expert on leveling up characters in every version of WoW Classic at this point, so I was able to lock in and move my way from level 1 to 60 faster than anyone else I know. In Ocarina , my memories from two decades ago, as well as years of watching "BEST ZELDA DUNGEONS RANKED" YouTube videos, have come back to me and I am breezing through the game at a speed that would have befuddled my younger self. The Forest Temple is clearly the best dungeon in the game, and maybe in all of Zelda , but I steamrolled through all of the twisty hallways, tricky Poe mini-bosses, and the Phantom Ganon boss fight. As a child, that fight took me ages.
The ease with which these games have come back to me could have been a letdown, but I'm having a blast. My instincts are better, my stick skills have improved, and my reflexes, though worse than they were say in my early 20s, are more honed from so many hours of games. What these two excursions into my own gaming past have taught me is that I have really been on a journey of self-improvement—I see know lame that sounds—and the sense of accomplishment I get now is not from finishing something, but from finishing it in style.

articles.title_orig: RydeMe, Sahara, and WhatUp: 'GTA 6' is stuffed with Silicon Valley's evil twins
articles.title_zh: RydeMe, Sahara, and WhatUp: 'GTA 6' is stuffed with Silicon Valley's evil twins
articles.content_orig:
The " Grand Theft Auto " franchise has long skewered American life with a parade of double entendres.
Take "GTA 5" as an example. Rockstar Games built Los Santos as a dystopic Los Angeles look-alike, where the high-end Westwood Boulevard becomes "Morningwood Boulevard." Players strolling past upscale retailers can overhear NPCs bragging about their wealth and cosmetic procedures.
"GTA 6" is no different — but this time, Silicon Valley is the butt of the joke.
The new game, which launched on Thursday, is full of techie doppelgängers: delivery services, ride-hailing apps, and social platforms that look familiar, but now have overtly sexual names.

articles.title_orig: European leaders present united front in push for peace in Ukraine
articles.title_zh: European leaders present united front in push for peace in Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
These updates have been closed.
Below, you can review the top news from the Coalition of the Willing meeting in Berlin on Thursday, 19th November, below:
Ukraine and three of its key European allies have reiterated their commitment "towards a comprehensive, just and lasting peace for Ukraine ," which they described as being "vital for the security of Europe."
In a joint statement issued after Coalition of the Willing talks in Berlin, the leaders of Germany, France, the UK and Ukraine condemned Russia 's "systematic escalation of its deliberate and indiscriminate missile and drone attacks against Ukraine's civilians and civilian infrastructure."
Ukraine's right to defend itself was highlighted, as were Russia's battlefield losses.
The four leaders condemned "Russian hybrid attacks across Europe" and said they "would increase their resolve to strengthen the defence of Ukraine, Europe and NATO."
Leaders pledged "long-term and comprehensive support" for Kyiv and said that Ukraineäs air defense capability was a priority.
Russia's funding of its war effort would be targeted through sanctions and "pressure on Russian oil and gas revenues," while efforts to impede Russia's shadow fleet would continue.
On Ukraine's security, the leaders said the country needed "robust and legally binding security guarantees in place, once a ceasefire enters into force."
The statement mentioned "a European-led Multinational Force Ukraine composed of contributions from willing nations and supported by the US," something that has proven to be a sticking point for Russia.
The leaders said they supported "direct dialogue" between Kyiv and Moscow with US and European participation.
Ukraine's right to choose its own security arrangements needed to be "fully respected," the joint statement said.
"As a first step towards a cessation of hostilities, the leaders called on Russia to agree to an energy ceasefire for the duration of the winter," the statement read.
US special envoy Jared Kushner said unity in Europe was clear in the talks and that support for Ukraine remained strong.
"What we came away from today with is really seeing that Europe is very united and very, very strong in their support of Ukraine," Kushner said. "We relayed this to President Trump."
Kushner said this would also be relayed to the Russian delegation and that there was "a real desire for peace."
Kushner said that Trump had joined the Berlin meeting by phone and provided an update on the talks in Shenzhen with President Putin and President Xi.
"He sent a very strong message to both of them on the desire for peace and would like to engage with both of them very aggressively to get there," Kushner said.
Kushner told reporters the talks with European leaders ⁠and ​Ukrainian President ​Volodymyr Zelenskyy had "made a lot ​of progress ‌on what those security ​guarantees ⁠can look like," as well ⁠as ​a post-war prosperity plan.
He also said Russia was "comfortable" with NATO-like security guarantees for Ukraine to end the war.
French President Emmanuel Macron said that amid Russia's continued attacks on infrastructure and "maximalist demands," the first priority was for Ukraine to be able to defend itself.
Macron said allies needed to ensure that Ukraine had everything it needed to resist and defend itself from Russian attacks.
"Faced with the maximalist nature of the Russian position, I believe we need to reopen the question of Ukraine's accession to NATO," Macron said in Berlin.
"Everyone who has the capacity to provide the means to defend and protect Ukrainian citizens must do so now," the French leader insisted, adding the priority was to deploy anti-missile systems and interceptors.
Macron said security guarantees were a "key element for our long-term negotiations" and the security plan it had already submitted should remain.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Europe should be part of talks going forward.
"America fully understands why strong and coordinated European participation at the negotiations is necessary," Zelenskyy said.
Zelenskyy said his country needed international support ahead of another winter and added that more work was needed to "push Russia to be more constructive in any negotiations."
He also said much work was done to make the Berlin meeting "as concrete as possible."
Zelenskyy thanked all partners and expressed gratitude to Germany, France, the UK, the US along with those who had come out in support of Ukraine.
Zelenskyy highlighted the importance of air defense and said that Russia's aerial bombardments were steadily intensifying.
Zelenskyy said there was no sign this would change as "the Russians have rejected every single proposal for de-escalation."
Zelenskyy said that it was "crucial" that the US "exerts influence on Russia."
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has pushed for Europe to play a role in helping secure peace in the war in Ukraine.
"Today we prepared for ourselves for possible peace talks," Merz said.
"These talks should comprise Ukraine, Russia, the United States and Europe," Merz said, adding that this format offered the best chance of securing peace.
The German leader said Germany, France, the UK, Poland and Italy would speak on behalf of Europe.
He went on to call the trilateral talks between the president of the United States, Russia and China today at an APEC summit a "photo op" and said such a "Yalta format cannot bring peace" to Ukraine.
Merz pledged "powerful support" for Ukraine in 2027 and mentioned the €45 billion earmarked for next year by the European Commission.
Merz said the level of support was being provided in order for Ukraine to be able to protect itself and that allies wanted the war to end.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said the future of European security would be molded by what was happening in Ukraine.
"The outcome of this war will shape security in Europe for a long time to come," Merz said in a post on social media platform X.
"Together with our partners, we continue our support for peace in Ukraine. That's why we came together today for the Coalition of the Willing," Merz said.
He accompanied his comments with pictures from roundtable talks of the "Coalition of the Willing" in Berlin.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he went over "key issues and needs" with German, French and British leaders.
Zelenskyy shared a video on X of his meeting with France's Emmanuel Macron, Britain's Andy Burnham and Germany's Friedrich Merz.
He said they discussed "countering Russian shahed drones and missiles, protecting the energy sector and infrastructure, as well as the diplomatic efforts."
"It is important that today's Coalition of the Willing meeting and bilateral meetings with leaders deliver results," he added.
Ukraine 's European allies are gathering in Berlin in a show of support just hours after three-way talks took place involving the presidents of the US, Russia and China at the APEC summit.
European leaders are pushing to be included in US-backed talks to end the fighting in Ukraine with US special envoy Steve Witkoff and the US president's son-in-law Jared Kushner in Berlin for Thursday's meeting.
"Mr. Putin is not our friend and will never ​be," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said in a comment aimed at US President Donald Trump, who referred to Putin as "my friend" at a meeting on Wednesday.
"I find it very incomprehensible that a US president wants to sit down with President Putin," Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen told ​reporters.
"I think Putin will be even more emboldened after today's meeting. He looks happy," she added. "Unfortunately, that is not a good sign for world ​peace. That is not ‌a good sign for Ukraine ... And therefore I think that what will come out of this is that he will hit us Europeans even harder, unfortunately."
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen promised the EU was united in its support for Ukraine.
"Only through strength can we achieve a just and durable peace," she wrote on X.
